In multiagent learning, the primary objective is to enable autonomous agents to learn optimal strategies within a game defined by its payoff matrix. Traditionally, this field has focused on Coarse Correlated Equilibria (CCE) learning, where agents learn a joint probability distribution over all possible actions. However, this approach suffers from a curse of dimensionality, as the sample complexity required to learn a CCE scales exponentially with the number of agents. To address this limitation, we introduce the concept of Correlated Equilibria with Regret (CER), where each agent learns only a marginal distribution over their own action space. We demonstrate that the sample complexity for CER learning is comparable to that of CCE learning, thereby offering a more efficient alternative. Furthermore, we show that the set of achievable CERs forms a convex set, which allows us to develop a novel, efficient algorithm for finding the optimal CER. Finally, we prove that the regret incurred by our CER learning algorithm is at most a factor of $O(\sqrt{T})$ worse than the optimal CER, and we establish a matching lower bound for CER learning.

We examine a stochastic epidemic model defined on a configuration space, where the limiting proportion of infected individuals at the outbreak's conclusion is analyzed. Specifically, we investigate scenarios in which the infection rate is either fixed or varies adaptively based on the current state of the system. When the infection rate remains fixed near the critical threshold, the limiting final infection fraction displays non-trivial stochastic behavior, characterized by discontinuities and a lack of differentiability. Conversely, when the infection rate is state-dependent and selected adaptively, the resulting limiting final infection fraction becomes deterministic. In this adaptive case, the function mapping initial infection density to the final fraction is strictly concave, possesses a unique maximum, and is continuous with differentiable properties at specific points near the critical threshold.

This paper investigates the existence of Cotton solitons within the context of almost Kenmotsu 3-$h$-manifolds. We first establish that a non-Kenmotsu almost Kenmotsu 3-$h$-M can only admit an expanding Cotton soliton, and subsequently demonstrate that such an implausible scenario cannot occur. Consequently, no shrinking or steady Cotton solitons can exist on these non-Kenmotsu almost Kenmotsu 3-$h$-M. Furthermore, we examine the specific case of Kenmotsu 3-$h$-M, proving that an expanding Cotton soliton exists if and only if the scalar curvature $S$ adheres to the relation $S = 2\lambda(2\lambda - 1)$, where $\lambda$ is a non-zero constant.

Achieving the fitting of parton distribution functions (PDFs) demands the incorporation of extensive sets of experimental data alongside theoretical predictions. To facilitate this, a unified framework has been established for processing both datasets and theoretical models, ensuring a consistent interface for the fitting procedure. This system features a modular design that supports various input modules, allowing for significant flexibility and adaptability. Furthermore, the framework integrates the necessary algorithms to execute the actual PDF fits.

In reinforcement learning, agents typically enhance their performance by utilizing historical data, a process known as off-policy learning. Although this approach is effective, it is not without limitations. A primary drawback is that the distribution of past experiences differs from that of future actions, leading to distributional shift. This phenomenon can cause the agent to overemphasize rare events while underrepresenting common ones, thereby creating a biased training dataset. Furthermore, the utility of older data diminishes over time, necessitating the prioritization of more pertinent recent experiences.

To address these challenges, the standard solution is to sample a uniform distribution of transitions from memory, a technique referred to as experience replay. However, this method is inefficient because it discards potentially valuable information by maintaining a biased dataset. In response, we introduce a novel approach that constructs a non-uniform, data-driven distribution over the replay buffer. This new method is designed to be unbiased, ensuring that the training dataset remains representative of the underlying data. Additionally, it incorporates mechanisms to mitigate temporal decay, thereby preventing the overemphasis of outdated information. Empirical evaluations across various environments demonstrate that this proposed method outperforms both standard experience replay and other existing state-of-the-art methods.

We introduce `libcommute`, an open-source C++14 library designed to handle manipulations of polynomial operators within quantum many-body theory. Built upon `boost::math::tools::symbolics`, the library offers a flexible and efficient framework for these tasks. It supports both abstract operator algebra and concrete realizations using Fock spaces. The project is freely available at https://github.com/QuiLi1998/libcommute.

We present a comprehensive study of the electronic structure in the iron-based superconductor Ba$_{1-x}$K$_x$Fe$_2$As$_2$ using angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES). Our analysis reveals a prominent, flat-band-like feature situated near the $\Gamma$ point within the Brillouin zone center. This finding contradicts recent theoretical predictions suggesting that such features in hole-doped systems are merely dispersive bands obscured by strong spectral weight from electron pockets. Furthermore, our results indicate that the flat band observed in hole-doped Ba$_{1-x}$K$_x$Fe$_2$As$_2$ is distinct from that found in electron-doped NaFe$_{1-x}$Co$_x$As; specifically, the latter exists at higher binding energies relative to the Fermi level and demonstrates greater dispersion along the $\Gamma$-M direction.

Recent work by two of the authors (along with A. Scrucca) demonstrated that the supersymmetry method in Gaussian random matrix ensembles can be extended using either a continuous or discrete representation of $SU(1,1)$. In this note, we contrast these two approaches and illustrate their application to several non-Gaussian ensembles, including the circular ensembles, the chiral GUE, and the chiral SU(N) NSE.

This study presents an updated measurement of the spin asymmetry in t-channel single top quark production, utilizing the dilepton final state from dilepton+dijets+dilepton events. Derived from data collected by the ATLAS detector at the LHC at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV, the dataset spans an integrated luminosity of 140 fb$^{-1}$ recorded between 2015 and 2018. The observed spin asymmetry is measured at $A_{spin} = 0.053 \pm 0.014 \text{(stat)} \pm 0.010 \text{(syst)}$. This result aligns with predictions from the POWHEG-BOX@NLO Monte Carlo generator, which models single top quark events with a virtual W boson. The analysis achieves a statistical significance of 3.8 sigma, surpassing the previous ATLAS measurement by a factor of 1.7.

Utilizing neutron scattering, this study examines the magnetic structure and spin dynamics of the metallic phases in $\text{La}_{2-x}\text{Sr}_x\text{CuO}_4$ at Sr concentrations of $x=0.15$ and $x=0.16$. At temperatures well above the transition point, the spin-lattice relaxation rate, $1/T_1$, exhibits a $T^2$ temperature dependence, a signature consistent with metallic behavior. Furthermore, the study observes a pronounced enhancement of magnetic fluctuations near the critical temperature $T_c$.

Conversational dialog systems have advanced significantly over the last ten years, largely due to the introduction of large-scale public datasets. However, the MultiTalk Dataset remains the inaugural such collection designed to support multi-turn interactions involving multiple simultaneous talkers. Comprising over 1,000 hours of audio-visual data, the corpus features native English speakers engaged in tasks like open-domain question answering, instruction following, and conversational reading comprehension. The talkers in the dataset vary in number (one to three), gender, and voice characteristics. To facilitate future research, we provide a comprehensive analysis of the data and introduce evaluation metrics for both automatic and human assessments. Furthermore, we present baseline models for each task type, establishing a necessary starting point for further development in the field.

This study investigates the optimal configuration of an intelligent reflecting surface (IRS) within a multiple-input single-output (MISO) framework designed for secure communications. In this model, a reliable source transmits information to a legitimate receiver while aiming to degrade the signal quality for an eavesdropper. The research specifically addresses a scenario where the IRS possesses only partial channel state information (CSIT), comprising both large-scale and medium-scale fading data. To optimize system performance, the objective is to maximize the secrecy rate by optimally tuning the IRS's passive beamforming coefficients. To achieve this, the work introduces a novel alternating optimization algorithm that jointly refines the beamforming weights and the phase shifts of the IRS elements. Furthermore, the authors derive closed-form solutions for the optimal phase configuration under two distinct conditions: when the IRS channel is known with certainty and when it is subject to uncertainty. Finally, the paper provides an analytical characterization of the average optimal secrecy rate by examining its behavior when the IRS channel uncertainty is minimal.

We present the first cosmological N-body simulation utilizing the modified gravity model $f(R)$, employing a scheme that linearly filters the Poisson equation via a function of the local matter density contrast. This approach allows for the direct computation of the gravitational potential within the code, eliminating the need for approximations typically used to handle the non-linear terms of the field equations. We validate the scheme's accuracy against previous $f(R)$ results and standard Newtonian gravity. Additionally, we investigate the impact of various $f(R)$ parameterizations on structure formation and assess the computational performance of the method.

This paper examines the connection between Gaussian free fields and the Dyson model, specifically the process of orthogonal polynomials on the unit circle. We examine the behavior of the Dyson model in the infinite volume limit and establish that the resulting Gaussian free field is not trivial. Furthermore, we confirm the existence of a unitary transformation within the Dyson process that yields an equivalent formulation involving the Gaussian free field.

WorkingWiki serves as a collaborative platform for software project development, supporting integration with various programming languages such as Python, Java, C/C++, and Ruby on Rails. This paper introduces an extension to the system specifically designed for R packages, with the accompanying R package `rWw` available on CRAN.

This study introduces a new theoretical framework for analyzing the interaction between thermoacoustic instability and flame noise. The proposed model accounts for heat release fluctuations resulting from both local and non-local acoustic pressure variations, alongside the impact of heat transfer on heat release. The analysis focuses on a simple laboratory configuration featuring a single, partially premixed, bluff-body stabilized flame. The model utilizes a flame transfer function to represent heat release fluctuations as a function of acoustic velocity and heat transfer rates. These acoustic velocity and heat transfer components are derived from the linearized Euler equations, incorporating the effects of acoustic attenuation and bluff-body geometry. The resulting linear model is solved to determine the system's eigenfrequencies and growth rates. The predictions of this new model are validated against experimental data from a bluff-body thermoacoustic rig operating with natural gas. The findings indicate that heat transfer effects are critical for accurately predicting flame noise and that non-local acoustic forcing is essential for correctly modeling thermoacoustic instability.

We introduce a new class of topologically protected stellar oscillations, termed "topological modes," which arise in stars possessing differential rotation and strong magnetic fields. These modes emerge from the interaction between magnetic field lines and the Coriolis force, creating an obstacle to angular momentum transport that prevents crossing specific latitudinal boundaries. Consequently, oscillation modes are confined to regions on either side of these boundaries. The locations of these boundaries are determined by the star's differential rotation profile and magnetic configuration, rendering them robust against minor perturbations to these parameters. Our findings indicate that these modes are ubiquitous across most stars, including main-sequence stars and giant stars. Additionally, we propose a novel observational test capable of distinguishing these topological modes from other types of stellar oscillations.

"Although extensively documented in both theoretical and experimental domains, the understanding of chimera states remains incomplete. This study focuses on a specific type of chimera behavior within an undirected network of networked phase oscillators, where nodes are partitioned into two groups: one exhibiting synchronized activity and the other desynchronized. We demonstrate that the presence of a second synchronization threshold generates a distinctive bimodal distribution of coexistence times, characterized by a significant disparity in modes. Furthermore, we reveal that the bimodal distribution's smaller component corresponds to transient chimera states, whereas the larger component represents stable, long-lasting coexistence. Finally, we illustrate how network topology influences the characteristics of both the transient and stable chimeras.

We examine the dynamics of clusters within extended-Hubbard and XXZ spin systems, contrasting them with the behavior of on-site clusters bound by repulsion in quantum gases. While on-site clusters typically exhibit dynamics similar to free particles, extended-Hubbberg and XXZ models generate multi-site clusters whose evolution diverges significantly. Specifically, these clusters display a transition from diffusive to superdiffusive behavior as size increases, accompanied by a reduction in internal coherence. This phenomenon is explained by the interplay between internal interactions and the motion of the cluster's center of mass.

We investigate the impact of ultralight dark matter on neutrinoless double beta decay ($0\nu\beta\beta$), specifically focusing on scenarios where the dark matter field couples to neutrinos via a derivative interaction mediated by a scalar or pseudoscalar boson. This interaction induces a time-dependent neutrino mass, which in turn influences the $0\nu\beta\beta$ amplitude. Our findings indicate that this mechanism generates a time-dependent oscillation in the half-life, with an amplitude contingent on the nature of the mediator, the ultralight dark matter field, and the neutrino mass eigenstates. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this oscillatory behavior can be leveraged to enhance experimental sensitivity to the coupling between dark matter and neutrinos.

The detection of ultra-high-energy photons originating from distant cosmic sources remains a significant objective in modern astrophysics. This study examines how such photons interact with the Sun's magnetic field, demonstrating that they can generate electron-positron pairs, which subsequently trigger extensive air showers within the solar atmosphere. These phenomena may manifest as observable X-ray and gamma-ray emissions, as well as the acceleration of cosmic rays.

Nonlocal gravity represents a recently introduced, intriguing modification to gravitational theory that incorporates nonlocal effects into the gravitational action. This paper examines the nonlocal gravity framework within the context of a static, spherically symmetric system. By analyzing this setup, we derive the corresponding nonlocal metric and calculate the metric's curvature components. Furthermore, we determine the components of the energy-momentum tensor for a specific system characterized by a point mass. Finally, this paper explores the implications of nonlocal gravity on the dynamics of a test particle moving within such a field.

Distributed storage frameworks typically rely on either strong or eventual consistency to manage conflicting updates. Strong consistency ensures data integrity but often sacrifices performance, whereas eventual consistency offers higher throughput at the expense of complex conflict resolution. This paper introduces the "Remove-Win" design framework, which supports flexible consistency policies by automatically handling conflicts through update removal. We demonstrate that this framework is applicable to a wide range of data structures, including key-value stores, queues, and trees. Our evaluation shows that systems built on "Remove-Win" achieve performance comparable to those using eventual consistency while maintaining application-level transparency.

We have created a new SNP database, named snpUnion, which aggregates all SNPs from the HapMap project and the International HapMap Consortium Phase III. This database is available for download at http://bioinfo.uthscsa.edu/snpUnion/. Our analysis highlights that 1.5% of all common SNPs (with a minor allele frequency $\ge$ 0.05) are located within DNase-I hypersensitive sites (HPS) in at least one cell type. Furthermore, 1.5% of trait-associated SNPs identified by genome-wide association studies (GWAS) also reside within these regulatory regions. We provide a downloadable file containing these identified SNPs, along with their genomic coordinates, associated traits, and the specific cell types where they occur within DNPS HPS.

This study examines small systems in high-energy physics, specifically proton-proton and proton-lead collisions at the LHC, with a focus on collective phenomena observed in high-multiplicity events. The paper reviews experimental data and theoretical frameworks addressing these systems, highlighting the significant challenges and opportunities they present for future research. The authors argue that these systems serve as an ideal testing ground for advancing our understanding of Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD) in both perturbative and non-perturbative regimes.

We present a new, systematic search for radio emission from neutron stars (NSs) in low-mass X-ray binaries (LMXBs) with long transient intervals. Our analysis targets the complete population of such systems using the Chandra Source Catalog Version 2.0 and the NRAO VLA Sky Survey (NVSS). We identified 1,008 candidate NSs based on X-ray spectral properties and extracted corresponding radio data from NVSS. Our findings reveal that 10% of these candidates exhibit radio emission, a fraction consistent with the radio presence rate observed in transient NS LMXBs. Furthermore, we observe a clear anti-correlation between the radio luminosity of these stars and their transient recurrence times. This discovery implies that radio emission serves as a diagnostic tool for the accretion state of neutron stars in LMXBs, specifically indicating that the radio-emitting NSs in this population are likely active accretors.

Wide binary stars serve as valuable probes for investigating gravity at the low accelerations characteristic of galactic outskirts, potentially revealing anomalies in the Milky Way's dark matter distribution or new forces. This study presents a new method to determine the deviation of gravity from the $1/r^2$ law using wide binaries, focusing on systems with orbital periods exceeding 100 years. We present a new, extensive sample of 1,000 radio sources located in the northern hemisphere, with a median redshift of 0.43, derived from the FIRST survey. This dataset is 10 times larger than any previous sample of its kind. We analyze the sources' polarization properties, including the median fractional polarization ($\Pi_{\rm med}$), the median polarization position angle ($\chi_{\rm med}$), and the dispersion of polarization angles ($\sigma_{\chi}$). Our findings indicate that $\Pi_{\rm med}$, $\chi_{\rm med}$, and $\sigma_{\chi}$ are largely independent of redshift, angular source size, and flux density. However, we observe a significant trend where $\Pi_{\rm med}$ increases for sources with angular sizes smaller than 5 arcseconds, rising from approximately 1.5% to 3%. This behavior mirrors the size-dependent polarization seen in optical sources and is likely caused by the alignment of radio source jets with the intergalactic magnetic field. Additionally, we examined the polarization properties of radio galaxies versus radio quasars and found no statistically significant differences between the two populations.

This study introduces the notion of geometric modularity for a collection of non-algebraic weights and demonstrates that if this property holds for infinitely many such weights, it necessitates the existence of infinitely many algebraic weights. Additionally, we establish a new criterion for the geometric modularity of non-algebraic weights involving the congruence of $A$-polynomials. As a corollary, we confirm the geometric modularity for non-algebraic weights associated with $p$-adic $L$-functions defined by Hida families over any totally real field.

We present a theoretical framework for describing the nonlinear optical response of ionic solids subjected to terahertz (THz) radiation. Our analysis centers on the fact that the circular motion of ions under THz fields generates significant inertial effects on electrons, which are essential for accurately predicting nonlinear phenomena. By incorporating this mechanism, our model successfully accounts for the nonlinear Kerr response and resonant absorption features observed in GaAs across the 2–10 THz range.

The theory of $\tau$-tilting theory, introduced by Adachi, Iyama, and Reiten in 2014, has become a vital area of study within the representation theory of finite dimensional algebras. This paper offers a comprehensive survey of $\tau$-tilting theory, with a specific emphasis on its applications to algebraic geometry and the study of cluster algebras.

This study introduces a new NLI-based metric designed to evaluate the diversity of conversational responses. We posit that the underlying task of NLI tasks serves as an effective proxy for assessing diversity within dialogue generation. Our proposed approach evaluates the relationship between a user's input and multiple system-generated responses using NLI models. By leveraging this method, we achieve superior performance compared to existing diversity metrics across various evaluation settings.

This study introduces a novel framework for automatically identifying hazardous lane change maneuvers using deep learning. The proposed system utilizes a lane detection algorithm to extract road lane markings and employs a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) to analyze video footage for potential dangerous lane changes. By leveraging the strong feature extraction capabilities of CNNs, the system achieves a 90.5% accuracy rate in classifying hazardous lane change behavior.

We present new observations of the T Tauri system T Cha, utilizing the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) to map dust emission at 1.3 mm and 3 mm wavelengths. Our data reveal a clear dust gap located at approximately 10 astronomical units (au), a finding consistent with previous observations from the Submillimeter Array (SMA). Additionally, we conducted optical and near-infrared observations using the Gemini North and Magellan Telescopes to obtain new spectra of the system's central star, T Cha A. By combining these datasets with existing literature, we constructed a comprehensive spectral energy distribution (SED) for T Cha A. Our analysis indicates that T Cha A is a very low-mass object with a mass of roughly 0.05 solar masses ($0.05\,M_\odot$). We further argue that rapid rotation is the mechanism suppressing sustained hydrogen fusion in this object, preventing it from evolving into a brown dwarf. Consequently, T Cha A likely represents a rare, young example of a hydrogen-burning limit star.

Amplitude analysis serves as a vital tool for investigating hadron decay processes, yet it faces significant challenges from instrumental effects, particularly those related to vertex displacement. This study introduces a novel method to address these issues by employing an amplitude analysis framework within an unbinned extended maximum likelihood analysis. We demonstrate this approach using the decay $B^0 \to K^+ \pi^-$, incorporating both signal and background components. For the background amplitude, we utilize a simulation derived from control samples, while the signal amplitude is determined via an interference analysis of $B^0 \to K^+ \pi^-$. Furthermore, we validate this new technique using $B^0 \to D^{*+} \pi^-$, a decay characterized by a large interference between neutral $B^0$ mesons and their antiparticles ($\bar{B}^0$).

This study introduces a novel model for the dynamics of radiative energy in fireballs, applicable to both the explosive and post-explosive phases. By utilizing this framework, we analyze the evolution of radiative energy and derive new invariants that distinguish the two stages. We further establish a new criterion for the transition between the explosive and cooling phases. Leveraging the derived dynamical equations, we calculate the total energy radiated by the fireball and introduce a new parameter, $E_{\rm new}$, which serves as a proxy for the total energy input. Finally, we demonstrate that this model accurately describes the radiation curves of gamma-ray bursts and supernovae.

Bipartite graphs are frequently used to represent relationships between two distinct sets of entities, such as users and items in a recommendation system. Consequently, visual clarity is paramount in bipartite graph drawings, making the minimization of edge crossings a primary objective. This study introduces a novel method for generating bipartite graph visualizations by projecting nodes onto a curved cylindrical surface. We formulate an optimization framework that determines the optimal placement of nodes to achieve the fewest possible crossings. Additionally, we derive a novel closed-form solution for the optimal node ordering that facilitates these projections. Our approach is validated through a comparative analysis against the standard force-directed algorithm, demonstrating significant improvements in crossing reduction.

Deep learning models have achieved remarkable success in various computer vision tasks, yet most current research focuses on balanced datasets. In contrast, real-world applications typically involve data streams with non-uniform class distributions, necessitating continuous learning from these streams. However, existing methods for incremental learning often fail to address imbalanced data effectively. This paper introduces a novel approach that combines prototype-based memory with a dynamic temperature mechanism to balance prototypes across classes during incremental learning from imbalanced streams. By adjusting the temperature, the model can either emphasize or de-emphasize distance metrics for specific classes, thereby managing class imbalance. Experiments conducted on four benchmark datasets demonstrate that this method outperforms current state-of-the-art techniques for learning from imbalanced data streams.

This study introduces a novel walking paradigm for thruster-assisted bipedal robots, where propulsion is generated by lateral thrusters positioned at the base of the feet. We define the "impulse-based gait generation" framework, which relies on generating discrete impulsive actions to create walking sequences. Our approach centers on a new methodology for synthesizing these individual impulses, utilizing a hybrid system model to represent the post-impact dynamics and a Lyapunov-based strategy to ensure post-impact stability. Furthermore, we address the generation of pre-impact trajectories through an optimization scheme that leverages the system's nonholonomic constraints. To demonstrate the framework's efficacy, we validate our approach with both numerical simulations and physical experiments.

Let $(K, v)$ be a valued field where the residue field has characteristic 0 and $\omega$ is a $K$-linear form on a finite-dimensional vector space $V$. We define the associated residue map $\partial_{\omega}: JV \to \text{res}(V)$, which sends an element to the coefficient of its leading term along the form $\omega$. Assuming the valuation $v$ is Henselian, we demonstrate that $\partial_{\omega}$ is surjective and that its image constitutes the leading forms of the Hilbert-Kfrench ring. Furthermore, we establish a criterion ensuring that $\partial_{\omega}$ is injective, with the resulting image identified as the leading forms of the $J$-power of the ideal of definition of a valuation ring. Finally, we observe that these results remain valid when $\omega$ is replaced by a valuation on $V$ that is equivalent to $v$.

This study examines performance-based side-channel attacks targeting simultaneous multithreading (SMT) architectures, specifically focusing on the Spectre-MT vulnerability. We introduce a novel method to enhance the Spectre-MT attack by utilizing performance degradation techniques grounded in data hazards. Our approach involves scheduling instructions in the victim thread to create hazards that disrupt the execution of instructions in the concurrent thread. Our experimental results indicate that this new method is applicable to a broader spectrum of workloads than the original Spectre-MT approach. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the new attack achieves a higher correlation coefficient with lower noise levels when executed in an SMT configuration with an out-of-order, out-of-line (OOO-OL) processor.

We examine the possibility of explaining the $g-2$ anomaly through the Higgs boson by utilizing the $125\,\text{GeV}$ resonance as a portal to hidden sector particles that couple to the Standard Model via Higgs mixing. We specifically analyze the impact of deviations in the Higgs couplings to top quarks, bottom quarks, and tau leptons on the anomaly. Our findings indicate that, even when accounting for current experimental constraints, the hidden sector can account for the $g-2$ anomaly if the coupling to the tau lepton is enhanced by a factor of approximately 2.5. Furthermore, we determine the necessary magnitude of the hidden sector coupling to the Higgs boson to satisfy both the $g-2$ measurement and various theoretical and phenomenological limits.

This parameter is determined by analyzing time-dependent CP violation in neutral $B$-meson decays, specifically those involving $J/\psi K_S^0$ and $J/\psi K_S^0$ final states. The analysis utilizes data collected from $711/\text{fb}^{-1}$ of $e^+e^-$ annihilations at the $\Upsilon(4S)$ resonance. An unknotting operation involves transforming a knot into the unknot by applying a specific local move. These operations are fundamental to knot theory, and their study has been ongoing for decades. This paper examines the 2-twist unknotting operation, demonstrating that the trefoil knot requires exactly two such operations to resolve. Furthermore, it establishes the minimum number of 2-twist unknotting operations needed for every knot with a crossing number of three.

We demonstrate that the rational semifield of a tropical semifield $(\mathbb{R}^n, \max, +)$, defined over $\mathbb{R}^n$ with operations selecting the maximum and sum, possesses a unique representation as a directed graph. This finding yields a fresh perspective on the geometry of tropical hypersurfaces.
This paper introduces a new class of Vassiliev invariants of order $2n$ for oriented links, which are distinguished invariants of minimal possible order for their respective groups.

Matrix multiplication is a cornerstone of computer science, yet its computational demands escalate rapidly as matrix dimensions grow, necessitating the development of ever more efficient algorithms. This paper introduces a novel method for matrix multiplication that leverages the bitwise operations of a programming language to enhance performance. By decomposing matrices into binary blocks and utilizing efficient bitwise logic to compute partial results, the proposed algorithm reduces the number of arithmetic operations required. Empirical evaluations indicate that this approach outperforms standard implementations, offering a practical avenue for enhancing performance in performance-critical applications.

This study examines a multi-agent system where each agent possesses a distinct task and seeks to minimize its own cost by selecting an action from a shared, continuous action space. We introduce a continuous extension of the classic binary-agent "Hiring" game, known as "Continuous Hiring Game." In this framework, agents execute tasks sequentially, with the second agent's cost determined by the first agent's choice. Our analysis establishes the existence of continuous equivalents to both the "Hire the Best" and "Hire the Worst" equilibria found in discrete versions of the game. Furthermore, we derive closed-form solutions for agent costs and demonstrate that these continuous strategies yield higher costs compared to their discrete counterparts.

Amplitude-based resummation is an emerging technique for elevating the precision of theoretical calculations in particle physics by systematically resumming large logarithms within scattering amplitudes. This work presents an application of that method to the production of a $W$-boson pair in proton-proton collisions at the LHC, specifically targeting differential distributions for the $W$-boson transverse momentum ($p_T$) and the dilepton invariant mass. We utilize the leading order (LO) amplitude as a foundational input to generate both next-to-leading order (NLO) and next-to-next-to-leading order (NNLO) contributions via amplitude-based resummation. Our findings demonstrate that this approach yields highly accurate NLO and NNLO differential distributions for $W$-pair $p_T$ spectra and invariant masses, closely aligning with results from full NLO and NNLO computations. Furthermore, this method offers a practical means to incorporate higher-order corrections into NLO predictions for various $W$-boson differential distributions, such as those involving $p_T$ in single-$W$ production, by leveraging the universality inherent in amplitude-based resummation.

Federated learning (FL) enables multiple participants to collaboratively train machine learning models using decentralized data without transferring it. This paper presents a robust FL framework designed to operate over unreliable networks, specifically addressing two key challenges: ensuring data privacy across horizontal and vertical partitions, and maintaining system reliability despite potential network failures. In this proposed system, each participant constructs a local model based on their dataset and transmits only the necessary components to other parties. Upon receiving these components, participants integrate them into their own models to generate the global result. Crucially, the framework encrypts all exchanged parameters to prevent eavesdropping and incorporates a recovery mechanism to handle partial data loss caused by network failures. We specifically introduce two distinct aggregation protocols tailored for horizontal and vertical FL scenarios. In the horizontal approach, only encrypted model weights are shared, whereas the vertical method requires participants to send specific subsets of their data. Additionally, we introduce a novel encryption scheme that supports additive homomorphic operations, allowing for the secure aggregation of models from various participants. Our results demonstrate that the framework maintains strong privacy guarantees, achieves low communication overhead, and ensures resilience against data loss resulting from unreliable connectivity.

Kernel methods are widely recognized for their effectiveness in solving various machine learning challenges, including classification, regression, and clustering. However, their requirement for constructing and manipulating a dense $N \times N$ kernel matrix creates significant computational and memory constraints, severely limiting their scalability to large datasets. To address these limitations, recent research has introduced sparse and low-rank kernel techniques that approximate the full matrix using only a subset of data points. While these methods enhance efficiency, they often incur performance losses in terms of predictive accuracy. In this paper, we propose a novel approach called the "kernelized Nystr\"om method" (K-kNystr\"om), which integrates Nystr\"om approximations with kernelized Kronecker products. K-kNystr\"om constructs a kernel matrix of size $N \times N$ by filling it with values sampled from a kernel matrix of dimension $K \times N$, where $K \ll N$. This technique yields a kernel matrix that is both accurate and of full rank, offering superior performance compared to existing sparse and low-rank alternatives. Empirical evaluations across multiple real-world and synthetic datasets demonstrate that the proposed method achieves state-of-the-art results in classification, regression, and clustering tasks.

This paper introduces a generalization of the wreath product applicable to any functor $F$ from the category of groups to itself, denoted as $G \wr_F H$. When $F$ is the trivial functor mapping every group to the singleton group, this construction reduces to the standard wreath product. We demonstrate that this generalized product yields a faithful representation of $F(H)$ within the centralizer of an image of $G$ inside $\mathrm{Out}(F(H) \wr_F G)$. Furthermore, we examine the conditions under which this constructed group is residually finite.

The age at which pulmonary valve replacement (PVR) is performed for Tetralogy of Fallot (ToF) patients significantly impacts their long-term health, yet the specific factors determining this timing remain unclear. This study utilized a nationwide, population-based Danish cohort to analyze the timing of PVR in 1,588 ToF individuals. The analysis revealed that the decision timing was driven by a combination of patient-specific attributes, including age, sex, and pulmonary artery anatomy, alongside physician-related variables. Notably, the influence of anatomical factors varied depending on the treating physician, and the time elapsed since the initial ToF repair emerged as the strongest predictor of when the valve replacement occurred.
