This study examines a class of phase-field functionals featuring a non-standard, degenerate mobility term. We establish the $\Gamma$-convergence of these functionals, as originally defined by Braides and Novaga (2000), under Ginzburg scale conditions. This convergence occurs both within the bulk domain and across interfaces of arbitrary codimension. Our findings extend previous work by Braides and Novaga (2005), which was limited to interface scenarios involving second-order normal curvature. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our results have significant implications for modeling phase transitions with mobility mechanisms found in biological systems.

This study examines a simultaneous wireless information and power transfer (SWIPT) architecture within a mobile data network, where a base station coordinates resource allocation for both information exchange and wireless energy harvesting among users. The system is modeled as a non-cooperative game featuring a two-tier structure: an upper tier handles data transmission via OFDMA, while the lower tier facilitates power harvesting. In this framework, each user autonomously selects an information harvesting mode, whereas the base station optimizes power allocation to maximize total network throughput. The proposed game is proven to possess an $\epsilon$-Nash equilibrium, with a constructive method for its identification. Furthermore, the paper presents a low-complexity algorithm designed to achieve this $\epsilon$-Nash equilibrium.

Feature Pyramid Networks (FPN) have become a standard for multi-scale object detection, yet they often fail to identify large-scale objects. This study reveals that such detection failures stem from the fact that FPNs are trained to rely on high-level semantic features, which lack sufficient spatial resolution to detect large objects. To resolve this, we introduce a new spatial feature pyramid that aggregates spatial information from multiple levels of the backbone network. Experiments demonstrate that this approach significantly improves detection performance for large objects compared to the original FPN, with only a minor impact on detection of smaller objects. Furthermore, this enhanced spatial feature pyramid improves detection accuracy for other object sizes and has been integrated into various detectors, including Faster R-CNN, RetinaNet, and SSD.

Conditional models are fundamental tools for analyzing multivariate data, specifically addressing scenarios where the distribution between two variables depends on the values of one or more additional variables. This paper introduces a novel class of multivariate linear conditional models capable of handling both continuous and discrete data. We derive the corresponding probability measure and establish connections to other related models. Furthermore, we propose a framework for parameter estimation using maximum likelihood methods and evaluate the performance of these estimators through a simulation study.

In this work, we address the problem of Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD), a critical task in natural language processing that involves identifying the correct meaning of a word within a specific context. Our approach utilizes a neural network architecture based on bidirectional long short-term memory (BiLSTM) units, which are trained to predict the appropriate sense of a target word given its surrounding context. Our dataset consists of 1,000 annotated sentences drawn from the Wikipedia corpus, utilizing the WordNet semantic framework. Experimental results indicate that our proposed model achieves a top-1 accuracy of 60.4% and a top-3 accuracy of 79.4%.

Understanding and carrying out real-world activities typically requires interpreting instructions conveyed through spoken language, text, diagrams, or a mix of these formats. To address this challenge, we introduce a novel framework for teaching and executing visual reasoning tasks by processing multimodal step-by-step plans. Our approach begins by converting each plan step into a set of visual grounding predictions, which are then refined using a specialized multimodal attention mechanism. This system was assessed on two datasets: VisualWikipedia, comprising 2,500 steps from Wikipedia infographics, and VisInstruct, featuring 2,100 steps from diverse images and screen captures. Our model outperforms current methods, showing particular strength in handling steps that integrate multiple modalities. Additionally, we provide a flexible architecture capable of managing various forms of visual reasoning supported by multimodal instructions.

We introduce a novel framework for analyzing network attacks, termed the "node-attack model," which integrates both local and global attack strategies. In this model, an attack initiates by removing a specific node; subsequently, all nodes directly connected to any previously eliminated node are also removed. This process continues iteratively until the network disintegrates into isolated components. We define a "avalanche" as the complete sequence of node eliminations triggered by an initial attack. Our framework enables the derivation of precise analytical formulas for key metrics, including the probability distribution of avalanches triggered by a single initial node removal and the expected magnitude of such avalanches when the starting node is chosen at random. Furthermore, we investigate network resilience under this model, specifically examining how the size of an attack required to fragment the network varies depending on whether the attack is local, global, or a hybrid approach.

This work examines the properties of semi-classical orthogonal polynomials defined by a generalized Airy weight function on the negative real axis, given by $w(x)=|x|^{\alpha}e^{-Q(x)}$, where $\alpha > -2$ and $Q(x)$ is either a linear term $cx$ (with $c > 0$) or a quadratic term $\frac{1}{2}cx^2$ (with $c > 0$). We derive explicit formulas for the associated recurrence coefficients and demonstrate that when $Q(x)=cx$, these coefficients align with those found in previously studied orthogonal polynomials of Askey. Furthermore, we establish connections between this family and both the generalized Bessel polynomials and the Meixner-Pollchek polynomials.

We introduce a novel methodology for analyzing and mitigating high-frequency noise in gravitational-wave data, addressing limitations in current approaches that often rely on excessive data truncation or suffer from sensitivity degradation. By employing a linear, time-invariant filter to remove noise across a broad spectrum, our approach preserves signals in the 1–2 kHz range, a frequency band where traditional filters are ineffective due to their narrow pass widths. We demonstrate the technique's efficacy using data from the LIGO Hanford detector, revealing a sensitivity enhancement of up to 2.5× at 1.5 kHz. This improvement is particularly significant given that detector sensitivity at these frequencies is primarily constrained by high-frequency noise sources such as scattered light and thermal fluctuations.

Extra-large scale (ELS) massive MIMO systems offer a promising solution for addressing interference in high user-density environments by leveraging spatial diversity. These systems utilize a vast number of antennas to serve multiple users simultaneously, enabling the suppression of interference through the combination of maximum ratio transmission (MRT) and maximum ratio combining (MRC). This paper investigates the performance of ELS massive MIMO under MRT-MRC schemes, specifically analyzing the impact of channel estimation errors caused by pilot contamination. We derive closed-form expressions for the achievable sum rate and the probability of meeting target signal-to-interference-plus-noise ratio (SINR) requirements. Furthermore, we propose a novel non-orthogonal pilot assignment strategy designed to minimize total downlink pilot power while satisfying specified target SINR thresholds. Our theoretical results are validated through Monte Carlo simulations, demonstrating that the proposed non-orthogonal approach significantly outperforms conventional orthogonal pilot assignment methods in terms of power efficiency.

Disk fragmentation has long been proposed as a mechanism for directly forming planetary-mass companions, yet the diversity of observed disk substructures remains largely unexplained. We present new ALMA data on the 1.3 mm continuum emission of the Herbig Ae disk around HD 163296, which exhibits a prominent outer gap and an inner cavity containing a bright, unresolved source. Our analysis reveals that the inner emission is spatially resolved, showing a complex morphology with a distinct crescent shape and a central dark lane. We propose that this feature arises from the interaction between the disk's inner region and the disk's spiral arms. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the outer gap is not empty but contains a low surface brightness arc of emission.

The GW190814 gravitational wave event, detected by LIGO and Virgo, resulted from the merger of a ~23 $M_{\odot}$ compact object with another of roughly 2.6 $M_{\odot}$. While the primary's nature is understood, the secondary's identity remains debated, with theories proposing it is either a low-mass neutron star or a light black hole. This study investigates the secondary's identity by analyzing the effects of strong magnetic fields on neutron star structure. We find that for the specific merger observed in GW190814, strong magnetic fields can stabilize neutron stars that would otherwise be unstable due to their low mass. Consequently, the data supports the hypothesis that the secondary component was a neutron star, implying the existence of stable neutron stars up to approximately 3.5 $M_{\odot}$ under such conditions.

We have examined the electronic structure of SrMnO$_3$ using a Hubbard model that incorporates both onsite and nearest-neighbor interactions, alongside a comprehensive analysis of the crystal field splitting. This splitting arises from the interplay between the onsite Hubbard $U$, the nearest-neighbor hopping $t$, and the nearest-neighbor Coulomb interaction $V$. Our findings indicate that the crystal field splitting is highly sensitive to $V$, a factor that is crucial for accurately modeling the electronic properties of SrMnO$_3$.

We introduce a method for executing frequency-robust entangling gates on two trapped calcium ions using two distinct red motional sidebands. This approach leverages the interference between carrier-induced and sideband-induced transitions within the two-level system framework. By carefully selecting the pulse duration and detuning, the technique generates an effective two-photon transition that is resilient to frequency shifts caused by heating and laser instability. Compared to conventional methods relying on a single red sideband, this entangling gate demonstrates significantly higher robustness against such perturbations. Numerical simulations indicate that the fidelity of the generated gate remains stable even when detuning varies by approximately 10 kHz.

The structural prototypical diversity of perovskites is substantial, yet the specific configurations that dominate the structural phase diagram of BaTiO$_3$ remain unclear. We address this by employing a machine-learning interatomic potential to conduct a thorough analysis of the potential energy landscape for BaTiO$_3$. Our findings reveal that the most stable configurations are the well-known Pm$\bar{3}$m (cubic) and A2$_{am}$ (tetragonal) phases, alongside a newly identified, energetically competitive structure with Cmc$\bar{2}$1 symmetry. Furthermore, we demonstrate that a limited set of structural motifs can effectively represent the broader potential energy surface. Specifically, for BaTiO$_3$, the Pm$\bar{3}$m, A2$_{am}$, and the new Cmc$\bar{2}$1 phases serve as the primary structural prototypes. These prototypes are defined by their local atomic environments and their connectivity via low-barrier pathways, a framework that extends to other perovskites with varying degrees of octahedral tilting.

We demonstrate that interactions within graphene can generate a diverse array of novel physics beyond the standard description of massless Dirac fermions. While graphene's low-energy electronic structure is conventionally modeled as two interlaced, massless Dirac cones with linear dispersion, this view overlooks significant limitations: the constituent electrons are not truly massless, their effective masses are highly material-dependent, and their spatial wavefunctions possess distinct characteristics. By explicitly analyzing these underlying features, we reveal how interactions can drive novel phenomena, including spontaneous symmetry breaking, the emergence of mass, and the formation of correlated states such as Wess-Zumino-Witten models, quantum spin liquids, and topological insulators.

The beta distribution serves as a versatile tool for representing continuous data confined to a finite interval, yet its standard form cannot accommodate interval data containing a pole (singularity). To overcome this limitation, we propose a novel interval-valued beta distribution by reparameterizing the data interval to create a bounded domain where the beta distribution can be applied. This new model is capable of fitting data with poles, and we provide a method for estimating its parameters. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this distribution is flexible enough to represent unimodal, bimodal, and even multimodal data shapes.

We examine the production of heavy neutral leptons (HNLs) in $B$-meson decays, specifically focusing on the channel $B^{\pm} \to K^{\pm} N$ and $B^0 \to K^0 N$. Our analysis utilizes the effective Lagrangian for HNLs, incorporating both vector and axial-vector couplings. We derive the differential decay width for $B^{\pm} \to K^{\pm} N$ and the differential branching ratio for $B^0 \to K^0 N$ as functions of the squared missing mass, $m_{miss}^2$. These distributions are sensitive to the mixing parameter $|U_e|^2$, the squared mass of the HNL, $m_N^2$, and the coupling coefficients. We further establish the relationship between the observed event rate in $B^{\pm} \to K^{\sq

We present a new, straightforward derivation of the spectral shift observed in the gyroscopic Sagnac interferometer, noting that this phenomenon is historically recognized as the transverse Doppler effect. Our approach relies on the Liénard-Wiechert potentials and the Lorentz transformation of the four-wave vector. By analyzing the light's frequency as measured by a rotating detector, we account for the detector's motion relative to the source and the detector's own frame. This method offers a fresh perspective on the calculation, which may prove beneficial for addressing other problems in relativistic optics.

This paper offers a new proof of the existence of a Weierstrass section for any algebraic group acting on an affine space, along with an explicit construction of the section. Our approach relies on an alternative characterization of these sections, which involves the existence of a specific regular element within the space along with a related regular map.

Although neural language models have achieved significant success in various natural language processing tasks, $N$-gram models remain highly effective due to their simplicity and low computational requirements. This study introduces a method to enhance $N$-gram performance by integrating contextual information from neural approaches. Specifically, we utilize a bidirectional long short-term memory (LSTM) network to generate probability distributions over possible $N$-grams conditioned on surrounding context. These distributions are then employed to adjust the traditional $N$-gram counts, resulting in a hybrid model that outperforms both standard $N$-grams and equivalent neural architectures on several datasets. Notably, this approach achieves superior results at an even lower cost than the neural models it surpasses.

Accurately aligning and reconstructing 3D faces remains a challenging task, particularly when facing occlusions and diverse head poses. This study introduces a novel framework designed to robustly handle these issues by simultaneously addressing face alignment and 3D reconstruction. Our approach leverages a dual-branch architecture: one branch extracts features from a frontal face view, while the other processes features from side views. These multi-angle features are fused to generate a comprehensive representation that remains robust despite occlusions and pose variations. Furthermore, we developed a new dual-view loss function that enhances the model's ability to recover occluded regions and accurately predict pose parameters. Extensive experiments indicate that our method significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques on both the 300W and COFW benchmarks.

We introduce a new class of fractonic excitations characterized by completely immobile mobility for their dipole moments, contrasting with previous fractons that only immobilize dipoles formed by specific pairs. This distinction arises in a three-dimensional dipolar fracton model defined on a cubic lattice, where mobility is permitted exclusively when dipoles align with the lattice's diagonal axes. Consequently, these new fractons exhibit completely mobile dipoles along a single direction while maintaining rigidity in dipoles oriented along the other two directions. We determine the model's exact diagonalization and identify its gapless fracton phase, which features a finite mobility tensor and supports a continuum of excitations with negative group velocity squared values. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this system displays a three-dimensional fracton version of the Dirac semimetal phase.

We investigate the early universe dynamics within the context of a scalar field theory featuring a Hubble-scale mass and a periodic potential, specifically examining regions where the field oscillates near potential minima. Our analysis reveals that field fluctuations can drive the field into chaotic motion, a process capable of generating substantial curvature perturbations. We demonstrate that if these conditions arise within a sufficiently large volume, they could lead to the formation of primordial black holes (PBHs) with masses around $10^{17}$ g, which would decay via Hawking radiation precisely when current cosmic structures began to form.

This study examines the structural characteristics of marked ordered trees, a class of trees defined by a marking function $f$ that assigns each node a value from $\{0,1\}$ based on its children's configuration. We analyze the distribution of deepest nodes within these trees, where depth is determined by the sum of markings along the path from the root. Assuming $f$ is non-degenerate, we demonstrate that as tree size $n$ grows, the count of deepest nodes follows a normal distribution with mean $2\ln n$ and variance $1/2$. We further examine several specific instances of $f$, including cases where the function depends solely on the number of children or specific patterns of immediate descendants.

This paper introduces Informed OCR, a novel system designed to enhance the capabilities of standard OCR. Unlike conventional approaches, which often yield subpar results, this method leverages the contextual knowledge of a Knowledge Graph (KG) to improve upon the performance of the best available OCR systems. The proposed framework operates in three distinct stages: initially, it identifies and retrieves relevant entities from the KG based on the input image content; subsequently, it constructs a tailored subgraph containing these pertinent nodes and edges; finally, it utilizes this focused subgraph to guide the OCR engine, resulting in improved accuracy. Experimental evaluations demonstrate that this approach significantly outperforms the strongest existing OCR models, achieving a 14.5% increase in F1 score.

This study examines linear regression models under scenarios where data exhibits long-memory characteristics. We analyze the convergence rate for both the bias and risk associated with the least squares estimators, covering cases with independent regressors and those where regressors form a stationary, linearly process with long-memory properties. Our findings indicate that the influence of long-memory data results in a notably slower convergence rate compared to independent settings. Furthermore, we introduce a novel class of robust regression models capable of addressing outliers and non-Gaussian innovations, specifically analyzing the asymptotic behavior of the proposed robust estimators.

Speech enhancement serves as a vital component of audio signal processing technologies, including speech recognition and synthesis. This study introduces a new framework for robust automatic speech enhancement that leverages deep learning. The proposed system utilizes a Deep Mixture of Experts (DMoE) architecture, which integrates a set of specialized acoustic models to create a system capable of processing diverse sounds. In this approach, the DMoE functions as a gating mechanism that dynamically routes input signals to the most appropriate expert. The study evaluates the method using the Deep Mixture of Experts for Automatic Speech Enhancement (DMoE-ASR) system, demonstrating its ability to improve speech quality in noisy environments.

This study introduces a new control strategy for Negative Pressure Rooms (NPRs) designed to minimize infection risks by maintaining negative air pressure relative to adjacent spaces. A novel nonlinear, state-space model of the NPR is developed, and a new feedback controller is designed to regulate internal pressure. This controller utilizes only pressure measurements from internal sensors and those from the surrounding area, requiring no data on room volumes or airflow resistance characteristics. Theoretical analysis confirms that the system states remain bounded and converge to a desired setpoint. Furthermore, the practical application of this controller is demonstrated through simulation results.

Storage resources are essential for maintaining grid reliability and are increasingly prevalent in power markets. However, the operational strategies of storage entities facing price uncertainty and risk aversion can significantly influence system reliability and overall welfare. This paper investigates the optimal dispatch of a single storage unit within a two-period model, analyzing how its actions vary under different risk attitudes. We find that a risk-averse resource will reduce electricity consumption during high-price intervals and increase consumption during low-price intervals compared to an optimal risk-neutral operator. Furthermore, the magnitude of these deviations from risk-neutral behavior is contingent upon the specific shape of the utility function and the level of price volatility. Finally, we demonstrate that a single observed storage dispatch pattern is insufficient to definitively determine whether the resource is risk-neutral or risk-averse.

We report the generation of attosecond soft x-ray pulses lasting approximately 300 as, accompanied by a 100-fold increase in spectral peak intensity. This advancement is achieved by employing a 1000 W/cm² linearly polarized infrared laser pulse within a 100 Gs magnetic field to enhance the strength of the induced electron dipole moment. The resulting spectral shift and intensity changes were analyzed using a time-dependent Schrödinger equation model, which indicates that electron dynamics occur on a timescale of roughly 300 as. This finding establishes an ultrafast soft x-ray attosecond pulse source capable of probing electron dynamics within various quantum systems, including molecules and solids.

This study examines the formation of multiple jets in a simplified, Earth-like atmospheric model utilizing a two-dimensional General Circulation Model (GCM). The model incorporates a simplified topography and surface albedo, with atmospheric dynamics driven by the interplay of diurnal heating cycles and planetary rotation. By varying the rotation rate, we observe that multiple jets emerge when rotation is sufficiently slow, a phenomenon arising from the interaction between diurnal thermal forcing and the resulting stationary waves. Specifically, the formation of these jets is attributed to the resonance between the first stationary wave mode and the surface albedo wave, which possesses a wavenumber of three. Furthermore, the study investigates how these multi-jet configurations respond to changes in heating amplitude and rotation speed, revealing that the jets are highly sensitive to heating intensity and exhibit significant asymmetry. This atmospheric asymmetry is driven by the nonlinear interaction between the stationary wave and the planetary westward mean flow.

Active learning (AL) aims to minimize data requirements by selecting the most informative samples for labeling, while self-supervised pretraining (SSP) leverages vast amounts of unlabeled data to initialize neural networks with effective representations. Although AL and SSP appear contradictory, they complement each other: AL reduces dependency on labeled data, whereas SSP utilizes extensive unlabeled resources to enhance model representation. This paper introduces a novel framework integrating AL and self-supervised pretraining (AL-SSP) to further improve performance on downstream tasks. In this approach, the system selects the most valuable unlabeled samples for initial training, followed by refining the model using remaining unlabeled data via self-supervised pretraining. Finally, the model undergoes supervised fine-tuning using the resulting well-pretrained network. Experiments on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 datasets demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art results, utilizing only 10% of the data compared to previous approaches while using only 10% of the data.

This note offers an explicit formula for the generalized algebraic multiplicity, first defined by S. Gabrielov, which is expressed as a ratio involving two quantities: the local intersection index of algebraic varieties and the degree of a specific algebraic mapping.

We introduce a quantum network architecture utilizing an array of atoms arranged in a one-dimensional cavity, where entanglement propagates via the swapping of virtual photons. Specifically, when two atoms interact with the confined field, their mutual correlation increases as the non-Markovian memory of the cavity environment persists. This mechanism allows for the exponential amplification of entanglement between atoms, a phenomenon characteristic of strong quantum effects within highly non-Markovian regimes. Furthermore, this model supports the generation of multipartite Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger (GHZ) states, with entanglement growing exponentially as a function of the system's size.

We examine the exchange interaction between two electrons occupying $s$-orbitals in silicon donors, specifically focusing on how it varies with donor spacing and orientation. By employing a variational approach that utilizes a variational wave function composed of hydrogenic orbitals, we examine the influence of electron-electron repulsion. Our findings indicate that this repulsion significantly alters both the magnitude of the interaction energy and the spatial distribution of the electron densities. Furthermore, we explore the role of electron correlation by analyzing the movement of one electron in response to the presence of another.

We present a theoretical investigation into the electronic properties of HgTe quantum wells subjected to a magnetic field oriented parallel to the well's surface. Our findings indicate that, contrary to the case of infinite HgTe films, the formation of helical edge states typically does not occur under these specific conditions. Instead, our analysis reveals the emergence of localized states within the bulk of the well, which are associated with the confinement of electrons in the growth direction. These newly identified localized states exhibit a distinct dependence on the strength of the applied magnetic field. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these features can be successfully modeled using a two-band Hamiltonian that incorporates both the relativistic spin-orbit coupling and the effects of magnetic confinement.

Vehicular communication protocols are increasingly vital for enhancing road safety and traffic efficiency, particularly at intersections where they facilitate the exchange of data among vehicles and infrastructure. However, the prevalence of malicious actors necessitates robust security measures. This study introduces a novel authentication protocol designed specifically for vehicular communications at roadway intersections. The approach integrates elliptic curve cryptography with a revocation mechanism to ensure secure interactions. Furthermore, the authors present an evaluation demonstrating that their solution effectively safeguards against various cyber-attacks while maintaining high system efficiency.

This study examines the performance of Dynamic Time-Division Duplexing (TDD) in cellular networks, where uplink and downlink transmissions are determined by base stations independently. The study models interference by considering that downlink signals interfere with uplink receptions at user equipment, and vice versa, without accounting for inter-cell interference within the same direction. The objective is to maximize downlink throughput by optimizing TDD configurations, treating cross-direction interference as a constraint. The paper introduces a novel stochastic geometric approach utilizing Poisson Point Processes to represent user equipment locations. It derives a closed-form expression for the signal-to-interference ratio threshold required to achieve a specific target throughput. The study also examines the impact of random backlinking on interference, showing that the proposed TDD optimization outperforms both random and cell-synchronous configurations. Finally, the authors validate their theoretical findings through Monte Carlo simulations.

Normal electric currents flowing through a superconductor typically generate a transverse voltage perpendicular to the current direction only when subjected to a magnetic field, a phenomenon known as the Hall effect. In type-II superconductors, a distinct variant called the "vortex Hall effect" occurs, where vacancies within a vortex lattice move in response to thermal fluctuations, creating a measurable Hall voltage. This study introduces a novel theoretical framework based on the concept of vortex fluidity to elucidate the origin of the vortex Hall effect. Our approach attributes the phenomenon to the motion of vacancies between vortices, which induces a Hall response within the surrounding normal electrons. Our theoretical predictions align closely with experimental data from high-temperature cuprate superconductors, specifically regarding the magnetic field dependence of the vortex Hall resistivity. Furthermore, our model successfully accounts for the observed non-monotonic behavior of the vortex Nernst coefficient with respect to magnetic field strength.

The critical dynamics governing the transition to the hadron gas phase in high-energy heavy-ion collisions are investigated using a Langevin model for the energy density and two additional order parameter components. By analyzing the system's behavior across the phase diagram, we identify a universal fixed point characterized by critical dynamics independent of the specific functional form of the curvature (inverse susceptibility) in the free energy. Furthermore, we examine the influence of significant thermal fluctuations near the critical point on the universal behavior, concluding that while these fluctuations shift the location of the fixed point, they do not alter its nature.

We demonstrate that every finite index, hyperfinite, hyper-abelian subgroup of the type II_1 subfactor $N \subset M$ can be expressed as the intersection of hyperfinite, abelian subgroups of $N \subset M$ with index strictly less than that of the original subgroup. This outcome serves as a splitting theorem for hyper-abelian subgroups within the hyper-finite type II_1 subfactor $N \subset M$, given the existence of hyper-abelian subgroups of $N \subset M$ with minimal index.

This study introduces a meta-learning framework utilizing ODE-based neural networks to model the optimization process. By representing the learning trajectory as a continuous system governed by ordinary differential equations, this approach offers an efficient, parameterized summary of the entire trajectory, thereby reducing memory consumption. This method enables meta-learning in scenarios where only trajectory data is available, without access to internal optimizer states. Experiments across various benchmarks demonstrate that this model outperforms traditional optimizers in both single- and multi-task settings, while also surpassing competing meta-learning algorithms. Additionally, it successfully adapts to new tasks using merely one gradient step.

Developing machine learning (ML) models that are both trustworthy and explainable is essential for enabling their use in safety-critical domains such as healthcare, transportation, and finance. This paper introduces a novel framework designed to enhance the explainability and reliability of ML systems. Our approach integrates feature importance analysis with a novel method for generating counterfactual explanations, which are inputs that are minimally different from the original input but lead to distinct predictions. Furthermore, we propose a new algorithm for creating realistic counterfactuals that simultaneously optimize multiple objectives, including the minimization of distance to the source input, adherence to data distribution constraints, and the avoidance of sensitive attributes. Experimental results on two datasets demonstrate that our framework produces superior explanations compared to existing state-of-the-art methods.

Detecting prohibited objects in X-ray scanners is a critical task for public safety, yet existing methods often overlook the dynamic nature of these detections. This study introduces a Dynamic Detection Framework (DDF) designed to identify contraband in x-ray imagery by adaptively refining detection regions. The core innovation of DDF is the Lateral Inhibition Module (LIM), which refines detection boxes by suppressing background areas surrounding the initial prediction. By applying lateral inhibition to eliminate irrelevant background noise, the model achieves more precise detections. Furthermore, the framework incorporates a Dynamic Detection Unit (DDU) to refine the detection boundaries of prohibited items. Extensive experiments on the XRay-CD dataset demonstrate that the proposed method surpasses current state-of-the-art techniques.

We introduce a new family of polynomials, $J_n^T$, defined as the $n$th toroidal colored Jones polynomial. This family exhibits properties analogous to those of the standard colored Jones polynomial, including the existence of a quantum cluster structure within its coefficients and adherence to the Fock-Rosly cluster pattern. Furthermore, we demonstrate that $J_n^T$ serves as a deformation of the recently introduced $T$-invariant Kauffman polynomial.

Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD) involves identifying the correct meaning of a word within a specific context, a critical task for numerous Natural Language Processing applications. In this study, we introduce a new WSD approach that leverages the structural properties of Word2Vec word embeddings. Our method constructs a directed acyclic graph (DAG) from these embeddings to capture the contextual nuances of target words. We then apply shortest path algorithms to disambiguate those words based on their paths within this DAG framework. Experiments conducted on two standard WSD datasets demonstrate that our method achieves performance comparable to state-of-the-art models, while also offering significant advantages in terms of computational efficiency.

This study presents a new integral representation for the reciprocal $\Gamma$ function as a multiple integral involving exponential terms and power functions with fractional powers. It is demonstrated that this representation holds for all complex numbers $z$ where the real part is positive ($Re(z) > 0$). Although similar in form to established identities such as the Meijer $G$-function representation, this result distinguishes itself by utilizing only elementary functions. Additionally, it is shown that this integral representation is particularly beneficial for enhancing the efficiency of numerical algorithms designed to compute $\frac{1}{\Gamma(z)}$.

In particle physics, the Higgs boson was discovered in 2012 following extensive searches initiated shortly after the Large Hadron Collider's opening in 2008. This discovery relied on a significance threshold of $5\sigma$, where one standard deviation corresponds to a $68.3\%$ confidence level. To achieve this precision, the CMS experiment developed the `HiggsAnalysis/CombinedLimit` package, which streamlines the generation of statistical limits for searches involving new particles or modified properties of known particles. This package utilizes `ROOT`'s `RooStats` and `RooFit` toolkits to facilitate statistical analyses. It supports both the classical $CL_s$ method and the approximate $q$-interval approach for limit setting. This document introduces a new feature in the `CombinedLimit` package: the capability to establish confidence intervals and limits using `RooStats`'s `FrequentistIntervalCalculator` with the asymptotic profile likelihood ratio technique. This addition offers users a flexible alternative to the traditional $CL_s$ framework.

We introduce SQL2Bench, a comprehensive, high-quality dataset designed for English-to-SQL semantic parsing. This collection comprises 18,000+ tasks across 140+ databases from 10 distinct domains, including newly added benchmark materials from the 2023 and 2024 editions of the SemEval SQL Challenge. Our dataset offers a rigorous test for current models, particularly in cross-domain transfer learning. Based on this benchmark, we propose a new framework that integrates domain-specific schema information with a unified language model. This framework utilizes a two-stage approach: first, a model trained on a single database generates an initial SQL query, and second, a trained model refines this query using the target database's schema. Experimental results indicate that this framework achieves a significant improvement in execution accuracy compared to current state-of-the-art methods.

This paper introduces a novel framework for privately analyzing graph-structured information. We propose a new definition of graph privacy that is both intuitive and adaptable to various graph analytics tasks. Addressing the challenge that standard privacy mechanisms like the Laplace mechanism are difficult to apply directly to complex graphs, we develop a specialized technique leveraging the graph's inherent structure. Our approach employs a hierarchical grouping strategy to achieve the necessary data utility by balancing privacy budgets across multiple levels of a graph's topology. The validity and effectiveness of our hierarchical graph privacy framework are demonstrated through a series of comprehensive experiments.

The Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope will commence operations in the mid-2020s, offering wide-field wide-field imaging across the near-infrared spectrum (0.55–1.05 μm) and high-sensitivity near- and mid-infrared spectroscopy (5000–25,000 Ångströms). These capabilities will enable the construction of extensive galaxy catalogs and the study of galaxy evolution across cosmic history. This work introduces a novel method for estimating galaxy stellar mass using the Roman Wide Field Instrument (WFI) and its Integral Field Spectrograph (IFS). The proposed technique utilizes a semi-parametric spectral energy distribution (SED) fitting method, which combines a parametric component to model the spectral continuum with a non-parametric component to represent emission lines. We demonstrate that this approach yields accurate galaxy mass estimates for both local and high-redshift samples. Furthermore, we illustrate how the synergy between Roman's wide-field imaging and high-resolution spectroscopy will facilitate the assembly of massive galaxy samples at high redshifts, thereby advancing our comprehension of galaxy evolution.

This study introduces a new framework for automatically generating virtual road networks tailored to autonomous vehicle safety assessments. Our approach utilizes a graph-based representation of the road network, where graph nodes correspond to specific geographic locations and edges denote drivable connections between them. By adjusting these control points, we create diverse network topologies that facilitate the systematic testing of various safety-critical scenarios. We developed an algorithm to compute the geometric changes in the network resulting from specific manipulations of these controls. Furthermore, we established a formal link between network geometry and the actual driving paths executed by the vehicle, utilizing this framework to enhance the efficiency of safety assessment procedures.

Descriptions are frequently employed to aid users in discovering and organizing music, yet existing user-facing tools often rely on generic, pre-existing song descriptions that can be inaccurate or irrelevant to specific collections. Furthermore, current methods for generating these descriptions typically involve manual effort or are limited to a single language. Addressing these shortcomings, we propose a system that creates multilingual descriptions tailored to a user's specific music taste. Our approach leverages an audio-semantic embedding model to construct personalized, low-dimensional representations of a playlist, which then feeds into a transformer-based sequence-to-sequence framework designed for multi-lingual generation. We evaluated our method against human-authored descriptions and a baseline model using a dataset of over 1,000 Spotify playlists. Our experiments demonstrate that our system achieves superior performance in both user preference and preference-based metrics compared to the baseline.

We apply the positive-P phase-space framework to simulate quantum many-body dynamics, with a specific focus on interacting Bose gases. Our study examines both the time evolution of expectation values and the dynamics of fluctuations within a 1D Bose glass system subject to a disordered potential and on-site interactions. Results indicate that the positive-P method accurately captures the dynamics of expectation values even with limited sampling; however, it requires significantly more samples than truncated Wigner approximations to fully resolve fluctuation behaviors. We further demonstrate that these required sample counts can be drastically reduced by leveraging a symplectic integrator adapted for the positive-P equations of motion.

Temporal action detection aims to identify the precise start and end times of specific actions within a video. This study focuses on the Two-Tailed Action Detection (TAD) task, which targets actions with variable durations that possess distinct initial and terminal segments. Common examples include actions like "hitting" or "kicking," where the event is flanked by preparatory and recovery motions. Although these actions are ubiquitous in daily life, current deep learning models often struggle to detect them effectively. This difficulty arises because existing methods typically treat the entire action duration as a uniform interval, failing to recognize that the head and tail segments possess unique temporal dynamics. Furthermore, the head and tail often exhibit significant visual dissimilarity from the central part of the action. To address these challenges, we propose a novel Deep Bidirectional Temporal Attention Network (BTDAN) designed to capture the distinct features of the action's head and tail. BTDAN utilizes two separate bidirectional temporal attention mechanisms: one to isolate the action's start and end points, and another to extract deep representations specifically for the head and tail sections. Additionally, we introduce a Bidirectional Temporal Attention (BTA) module that functions as a dual-gating system to dynamically integrate deep features from both the action's boundaries and its core. Experiments on the TAD-2019 benchmark demonstrate that BTDAN achieves a mean average precision (mAP) of 34.8%, surpassing previous state-of-the-art results.

This study examines the parallel current structures in the edge of the plasma, specifically those associated with the H-mode transition. By analyzing the radial profiles of the parallel current density, $j_{||}$, and the toroidal rotation velocity, $V_{\phi}$, derived from the RMP-induced perturbation analysis of the Motional Stark Effect (MSE) data, we identify that these features are localized within magnetic islands. These findings align with the hypothesis that the transition is driven by the tearing of the $n=2$ mode. Furthermore, we observe that $j_{||}$ exhibits a strong radial correlation with $V_{\phi}$, which we attribute to the radial electric field generated by the $\mathbf{E}\times\mathbf{B}$ drift within the island. The presence of these structures is most pronounced in cases where RMPs trigger a partial transition, resulting in a distinct H-mode pedestal. We propose that these features represent localized versions of the broader structures observed during the global transition. Finally, we discuss the potential significance of these localized current and flow anomalies in the context of the magnetic island-mediated H-mode transition theory.

This paper addresses collision avoidance for non-holonomic robots traveling at constant linear velocities within a 2-D plane. We introduce a new class of time-invariant vector fields, termed "safe fields," which generate collision-free trajectories. By employing a switching strategy that selects among these fields, we guarantee the avoidance of collisions. Furthermore, we propose a specific switching rule that enables a robot to reach any target position while evading obstacles. Our approach is validated through simulations.

This work establishes the annealed large deviation principle for the uniform distribution over the discrete torus $\mathbb{T}_n^d = (\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z})^d$ within the limit of $n \to \infty$. The principle applies to local empirical measures derived from random walks on $\mathbb{T}_n^d$ with arbitrary step distributions. We demonstrate that the associated rate function is precisely $q$ times the specific relative entropy between the empirical measure and the uniform distribution. Furthermore, we address a broader scenario involving step distributions that depend on time and prove a corresponding large deviation result for the set of empirical local times.

Intelligent Reflecting Surfaces (IRS) have recently emerged as a promising technology for enhancing wireless systems, including radar applications. This paper investigates the potential of IRS-enhanced radar systems, specifically examining a scenario where an IRS-equipped transmitter and receiver simultaneously transmit and receive signals toward a target. We analyze the impact of IRS configurations on target parameter estimation, with a focus on designing an optimal passive beamforming strategy for the IRS. Our analysis reveals that, for a single-ray model, the optimal beamforming approach is straightforward to derive. Furthermore, in the multi-ray environment, we demonstrate that the optimal beamforming design is equivalent to maximizing the received signal power. Our numerical results indicate that an IRS-enhanced radar system can achieve a 100% increase in received signal power and a 100% improvement in the Fisher Information Matrix (FIM) compared to a system without IRS.

Fuzzing has emerged as a key technique for uncovering security flaws in software, yet its effectiveness relies heavily on the quality of input mutations. Although fuzzers have historically used random mutation strategies, there is a need to evaluate whether this approach is optimal. To address this, we introduce a framework designed to assess the efficacy of various test input generation methods by analyzing the resulting programs for mutations. Our framework employs a novel, automated approach to determine the mutability of software components, specifically measuring the likelihood that a change in a component's value will trigger a failure. We utilize these insights to develop a learning-based fuzzing framework that utilizes Bayesian inference to infer the mutability of input components. This framework automatically generates test cases by altering the most probable mutable components, thereby enhancing the ability of fuzzing tools to detect bugs. Our framework is compatible with multiple existing fuzzing engines, including libFuzzer, Honggfuzz, and AFL, and has been integrated into libFuzzer. Our approach learns the mutability of components within a week, enabling the creation of test cases that are significantly more effective at finding bugs than those produced by random mutation.

This study introduces CoCoL, a method designed for continual learning in image classification that utilizes frozen, pretrained models. This approach offers a practical alternative to standard transfer learning by eliminating the need for extensive, task-specific pretraining. In contrast to other techniques that rely on additional labeled data or access to the original pretrained weights, CoCoL functions as a self-contained solution using only the pretrained architecture. It achieves this by employing a lightweight adapter network to inject task-specific knowledge into the frozen backbone. Experiments conducted on standard benchmark datasets demonstrate that this method surpasses the performance of other leading approaches.

This paper offers a novel proof demonstrating that locally area-minimizing surfaces within $\mathbb{R}^3$ possess locally H\"older continuous second fundamental forms with H\"older exponent $\alpha \in (0,1)$, where $\alpha$ depends on the minimum density. This result improves upon the earlier contribution by De Giorgi and Miranda, which established only uniform $C^2$-boundedness. Our methodology diverges from De Giorgi's original approach; instead, we employ a modern, streamlined version of the monotonicity formula originally developed by Allard. This refined formula enables us to derive essential estimates directly from the definition of minimal surfaces, thereby circumventing the need for the intricate blow-up and convergence arguments characteristic of earlier techniques.

This study introduces the concept of quasiperiodic solutions for semilinear parabolic equations with compact support, where the solutions exhibit uniform boundedness and remain within a compact set. We demonstrate that if a sequence of such solutions is quasiperiodic with respect to time, it admits a subsequence that converges uniformly on compact subsets to a limiting quasiperiodic solution. Furthermore, we examine the uniqueness of these solutions under specific conditions.

These studies reveal several new excited states, including a 10+ state at 10.01 MeV, a 12+ state at 10.02 MeV, and a 14+ state at 10.03 MeV. We introduce a novel method for selecting machine learning model parameters that is both simple and efficient, addressing the primary drawback of traditional K-fold cross-validation: its computational expense. Although standard K-fold is robust against overfitting, the necessity of training and evaluating the model multiple times for each parameter combination renders the process prohibitively slow, particularly for complex systems like deep neural networks. Our proposed approach utilizes a single training run to generate several distinct estimates of model performance, thereby reducing the overall cost. Empirical evaluations on both real-world datasets and synthetic data demonstrate that this technique achieves performance comparable to K-fold cross-validation while being significantly more efficient.

Deep neural networks have achieved remarkable success across numerous domains, including image classification, object detection, and natural language processing. A significant avenue for advancing these architectures involves leveraging pre-trained models to impart knowledge to new ones. Among these methods, the Teacher-Student framework stands out as a prominent approach for knowledge distillation. This paper presents an overview of Teacher-Student structures used in learning knowledge, highlighting their key applications, recent advancements, and potential future directions.

This paper introduces a novel approach to modeling graphical structures within reinforcement learning by employing deterministic finite state automata (FSA) to represent transition functions. We demonstrate that utilizing FSAs to encode transition functions is advantageous because it yields a compact representation, facilitates the application of efficient search algorithms, and supports modular learning. We propose a reinforcement learning algorithm designed to discover hidden Markov models (HMMs) by observing unlabelled trajectories; this algorithm learns an HMM that captures the underlying transition function of the environment. We further present a method for adapting this HMM into a policy that maximizes the expected cumulative reward. Experimental results indicate that this proposed policy outperforms a standard random policy and achieves performance comparable to that of a known optimal policy.

Photon recoil in ultracold matter introduces a new scale of variation, which significantly alters the standard Beer-Lambert absorption law. This paper examines how recoil modifies the absorption profiles of light traversing ultracold atomic or molecular samples. We demonstrate that recoil causes a broadening of the absorption feature in both velocity and spatial domains, with the resulting profile's shape contingent on the interplay between atomic recoil and Doppler effects. Furthermore, we show that by tuning the laser detuning, photon recoil can be harnessed to generate asymmetric spatial structures within the absorption features.

Dense, highly viscous suspensions are essential in numerous industrial processes, yet their complex rheological behavior remains only partially understood. This study employs molecular dynamics simulations to examine the structural and rheological evolution of dense suspensions under shear stress, utilizing a coarse-grained model that incorporates both shear- and short-range repulsive interactions. Our findings reveal that the transition from liquid-like to solid-like behavior is marked by a shift in dominant interparticle forces from shear-induced to shear-independent short-range repulsion. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the model's ability to accurately predict the shear thickening transition relies on the specific functional form of these shear-independent repulsive interactions.

We investigate a bilayer Heisenberg antiferromagnet subject to a periodic potential and a periodic Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya (DM) interaction, analyzing how varying system parameters drives transitions among antiferromagnetic, twisted superfluid, and twisted supersolid phases. Our findings indicate that periodic driving enables the emergence of these alternative phases even when conventional long-range magnetic order persists. Specifically, increasing the periodicity of the DM interaction lowers the critical threshold required for the transition to the twisted states. Furthermore, both interlayer and intralayer DM contributions are essential for stabilizing the twisted superfluid and twisted supersolid phases relative to the antiferromagnetic ground state. We validate these conclusions using both mean-field theory and Monte Carlo simulations, which demonstrate strong agreement.

This study examines the likelihood of WIMP scattering within an astrophysical halo as a function of the scattering angle relative to the halo's center, revealing a strong dependence on the nuclear recoil angle. We propose that this variation can be utilized to refine WIMP parameter constraints by incorporating scattering angle information into likelihood analyses. Our methodology involves Monte Carlo simulations of dark matter halos to model WIMP phase-space distributions across different recoil angles, demonstrating that scattering angle serves as a sensitive indicator of WIMP mass and velocity. We further illustrate how these findings can enhance exclusion limits using the case of XENON1T constraints on the p-wave scattering channel in the LUX-ZEPLIN experiment.

This study investigates the extent to which search engine personalization influences users' information access and their ability to locate pertinent content. We developed a novel methodology to quantify the degree of personalization inherent in services like Google and Yahoo! News, utilizing it to analyze actual search results. Our findings reveal that these platforms curate results to such an extent that up to 40% of relevant information may be omitted. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this hidden information varies significantly based on the specific user profile applied, with certain profiles potentially overlooking more than half of the relevant content.

This study proposes the construction of a next-generation facility comprising a 100 TeV muon-proton and 100 TeV muon-nucleon (likely intended as nucleus) collider. Such an installation would enable a wide array of crucial experiments in nuclear and particle physics, including precision measurements of the strong force, the determination of the proton and neutron radii, investigations into the origin of nuclear binding energy, and the search for physics beyond the Standard Model. To achieve these scientific objectives, we have developed a comprehensive simulation framework for the 100 TeV muon-proton and muon-nucleus colliders. This code simulates the complete beamline, interaction point, and detectors, specifically addressing the effects of beam-beam interactions and the utilization of opposing beam bunches to enhance luminosity. Additionally, we have determined optimal operational parameters for the facility, such as bunch population, transverse beam sizes, and the number of bunches per beam.

To address respiratory motion in MRI, a technique known as Respiratory-Adjusted Parallel Imaging (RA-RA) was created. This method utilizes a single-shot, highly accelerated Echo Planar Imaging (EPI) sequence. The acquisition process involves a single trajectory that is repeated at multiple respiratory phases, with each repetition employing distinct parallel imaging acceleration factors. The resulting dataset is reconstructed into a four-dimensional volume encompassing three spatial dimensions and one respiratory dimension. Subsequently, this volume is resampled onto a Cartesian Cartesian grid to facilitate conventional k-means clustering. The primary advantage of RA-RA is its ability to generate a motion classification map, which assigns a specific motion class to every voxel. This classification map is subsequently utilized to reconstruct the final images. The method was evaluated using a phantom study and validated in vivo using a healthy volunteer.

This study introduces a novel Input Constrained Control Barrier Function (ICCBF) to address safety-critical control problems involving general nonlinear, time-varying input constraints. By defining a specific subclass of feedback controllers known as ICCBF-based controllers, the authors establish conditions under which ICCBF-based controllers guarantee forward invariance of the safe set. Leveraging this theoretical framework, an optimized controller is constructed to simultaneously achieve safety objectives and additional task goals. This optimization is formulated as a Quadratic Program (QP) that incorporates both nonlinear time-varying input constraints and a cost function representing desired tasks. The proposed approach is validated through two illustrative examples.

This study examines CF-approximation spaces by characterizing CF-equivalence relations via CF-approximable relations. It demonstrates that the category formed by CF-equivalence relations is isomorphic to that of CF-approximation spaces, with the character function serving as the mapping between them. Furthermore, the concept of continuity for maps involving these spaces is generalized. Finally, by reinterpreting CF-equivalence relations through CF-approximable relations, the category of CF-approximation spaces is proven to be isomorphic to the category of complete lattice-valued closed relations.

Statistical significance testing is essential for evaluating and comparing systems in natural language processing. Historically, the paired-permutation test has been the standard method for determining if performance differences between two systems are significant, yet this test relies on assumptions that are often unverified. This paper examines the validity of the paired-permutation test by analyzing its underlying assumptions and comparing it against the bootstrap method. Our findings indicate that the paired-permutation test is valid only when both systems achieve performance levels near random chance and when their error distributions are similar. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the bootstrap method yields more reliable outcomes than the paired-permutation test in the majority of practical scenarios.

This study examines the "container crisis," a phenomenon that emerged in the mid-2010s and significantly disrupted the shipping industry. The crisis was precipitated by a sudden, sharp decline in demand that occurred despite a global economy showing robust growth. We analyze the phenomenon through the lens of complex systems theory, utilizing a supply-demand framework to model the system. Our analysis reveals that the crisis resulted from a mismatch between supply and demand, where supply outpaced demand following a sharp contraction. We demonstrate that the observed dynamics align with the classic "boom and bust" cycles characteristic of systems exhibiting supply-demand imbalances. Furthermore, we show that the crisis was not merely a passive reaction to demand fluctuations; rather, supply-side decisions actively amplified the downturn. Specifically, supply adjustments lagged behind demand changes, and the magnitude of these supply responses exceeded what demand variations alone would justify, thereby intensifying the volatility of the market.

We introduce the concept of a "loom space," which serves as a generalization of both linkless embedding spaces and those defined by linear inequalities. Specifically, a loom space consists of all points in $\mathbb{R}^n$ satisfying a set of linear inequality constraints where the coefficients of the variables are either $0$, $1$, or $-1$. This paper examines the topological properties of such spaces, with a primary focus on their homology groups. As a concrete outcome, we derive a simplified formula for computing the homology groups of loom spaces that generalize those previously established for linkless embedding spaces.

Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have achieved significant success in tasks like molecular property prediction and graph classification by leveraging graph structures. However, these models often struggle with data efficiency, requiring vast amounts of training data to reach high performance. This paper introduces Kedge, a novel data-efficient approach that enhances GNNs through edge augmentation. Specifically, Kedge generates new synthetic edges by combining existing graph structures using random walks and graph kernels. We evaluated Kedge on three molecular property prediction datasets, demonstrating that it boosts performance by 3% to 10% compared to state-of-the-art data-efficient baselines. Importantly, this improvement is achieved with only a 2% average increase in training data size and a 1.5x average rise in training time. Notably, when applied to the standard training dataset, Kedge delivers a 3% to 15% performance gain over current baselines without any additional data.

CountSketch serves as a method for creating data structures that enable approximate aggregation and querying on high-dimensional vectors. This paper introduces an extension of CountSketch designed to handle queries involving multiple data points simultaneously. We demonstrate the utility of this extended technique by accelerating various applications, including the estimation of heavy-hitters, join operations, and subgraph counts.

We have examined the thermoelectric response of a liquid composed of superconducting vortices under a longitudinal temperature gradient. Our findings indicate that the transverse Nernst effect exhibits a peak at a specific vortex density, which corresponds to the maximum superfluid density. Furthermore, the effect's temperature dependence reveals that the peak occurs at a temperature $T_{max}$ where the vortex-liquid's shear viscosity reaches a maximum.

This paper proposes a novel control strategy, termed two-stage predictive control (TPC), designed to resolve key limitations inherent in model predictive control (MPC). A primary shortcoming of MPC is its tendency to exhibit chattering and slow convergence when operating near a constrained equilibrium point. While recent efforts have attempted to address this by integrating an MPC framework with a separate local controller, these approaches often require specific tuning of parameters. In contrast, our proposed TPC method leverages the structural advantages of MPC by combining it with a computationally efficient, model-based optimal controller. Specifically, TPC functions by first utilizing an MPC algorithm to compute an initial control input, followed by a correction step that refines this input via a minimal adjustment. This architecture allows TPC to maintain the inherent benefits of MPC while significantly reducing the need for manual parameter adjustment. Furthermore, we demonstrate through a constrained optimization analysis that TPC is mathematically equivalent to a penalized predictive control (PPC) approach. Finally, convergence properties for both TPC and PPC are established within a constrained setting, and numerical simulations confirm the superior performance of these methods compared to standard MPC.

This study examines the impact of news sentiment derived from headlines and content on stock market prices. We developed a novel approach to extract sentiment from both news articles and their corresponding headlines using a Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT)-based model. Our methodology involves training separate sentiment classifiers on the content of each news article and its associated headline. We then apply an ensemble technique that integrates sentiment scores from both the article and headline classifiers to generate a comprehensive sentiment metric. Empirical analysis reveals that this combined sentiment measure exhibits a stronger correlation with stock price movements compared to sentiment calculated from either the article or headline in isolation.

The common envelope (CE) phase represents a pivotal stage in binary evolution, occurring when one star expands to engulf its companion. During this phase, orbital energy dissipates, leading to significant orbital shrinkage and potentially the ejection of the envelope. This process is crucial for generating various stellar remnants, including close white dwarf binaries, compact triple systems, merging neutron star or black hole binaries, and planetary-mass objects.

Although the fundamental physics of the CE phase are not yet fully understood, it is generally modeled as driven by the formation of a shocked, high-velocity wind around the intruding star due to its motion through the envelope. This flow extracts orbital energy to propel the envelope outward. A key unresolved issue is the efficiency of this energy extraction, which is parameterized by the $\alpha$-CE formalism. This formalism relies on the binding energy of the envelope and an efficiency parameter $\alpha_{CE}$, which remains poorly constrained.

To address this uncertainty, we present a new method for estimating $\alpha_{CE}$ by utilizing the specific angular momentum of the envelope. This approach is grounded in the assumption that the CE phase terminates when the specific angular momentum of the ejected envelope equals that of the surviving inner binary. We applied this method to a dataset of 1,000 observed planetary-mass binaries in the globular cluster 47 Tucanae.
