We analyze the longitudinal contribution to double Higgs boson production via gluon fusion within the Higgs Effective Field Theory (HEFT). Our analysis demonstrates that, at center-of-mass energies in the multi-TeV range, this longitudinal component becomes substantial and cannot be disregarded. We evaluate the magnitude of this contribution by comparing double Higgs production cross-sections computed in full Standard Model theory and in HEFT. Furthermore, we examine the sensitivity of future colliders to the effective field theory parameters $\bar{c}_{\bar{H}}$ and $\bar{c}_{\bar{H}}$ specifically through their impact on the longitudinal production amplitude.

We present a covariant expansion of the Einstein-Hilbert action around a fixed background metric, retaining terms up to second order in the metric perturbation. By applying this derived expansion to scenarios involving constant and linear Hubble parameters, we calculate the corresponding slow-roll inflationary models and their associated observables. Specifically, we determine the scalar spectral index, tensor-to-scalar ratio, and the power spectrum for both scalar and tensor perturbations as functions of the perturbation order. Our findings indicate that higher-order contributions significantly influence inflationary predictions, with the linear approximation (first order) yielding results closely aligned with those of the full second-order calculation.

We expand the Einstein equations in transverse gradients to all orders within a five-dimensional asymptotically AdS setting featuring an AdS$_3$ boundary. By expressing the bulk metric as a series involving powers of transverse gradients, we derive bulk equations that determine the coefficients of this expansion. Our findings indicate that, contrary to the belief held in the literature, these bulk equations are not solvable at any finite order. Instead, we demonstrate that the relation between bulk and boundary data persists as an infinite series, which we show can be resummed into a closed form. This result provides a new, exact bulk reconstruction formula applicable to higher-spin gravity theories.

We examine the forces acting on a cylindrical intruder falling through a two-dimensional granular assembly, utilizing both discrete element simulations and experiments conducted with glass beads. By varying the intruder's shape anisotropy, we determine the drag forces parallel and perpendicular to the long axis. Our findings reveal that the ratio of parallel to perpendicular drag, $F_{\parallel}/F_{\perp}$, increases as the intruder becomes more elongated. Furthermore, this ratio is sensitive to packing fraction and intruder size, yet remains largely unaffected by the granular material's friction coefficient. We propose that this behavior stems from the intruder's ability to generate a stronger force chain network along its length when $L/D$ is high, thereby enhancing parallel drag. Additionally, we demonstrate that the discrete element model accurately replicates these phenomena.

We present new observations of the ionized gas outflows in the starbursting galaxy NGC 253, utilizing the H$\alpha$ line to map the spatial distribution of outflow velocities and mass fluxes. Our analysis indicates that the galaxy hosts two distinct outflows: a large-scale, low-velocity component extending approximately 1.5 kpc from the nucleus, and a smaller, high-velocity structure confined to the inner 200 pc. We determined the mass fluxes for these components to be $1.1 \times 10^{-3} M_{\odot} \text{ kpc}^{-2} \text{ yr}^{-1}$ and $1.1 \times 10^{-1} M_{\odot} \text{ kpc}^{-2} \text{ yr}^{-1}$, respectively. Furthermore, we compared these findings with existing literature data on NGC 253 and other starbursting galaxies, revealing a positive correlation between outflow mass flux and star formation rate (SFR) surface density. This relationship suggests that the relative mass fluxes of the high- and low-velocity outflows are regulated by the SFR surface density.

Automated tuning of computer system configurations is vital for maximizing performance and efficiency, yet it remains difficult because the configuration space is vast, the search process is expensive, and the underlying relationships are often complex and non-linear. While Bayesian Optimization has emerged as a leading method for addressing these challenges, it typically struggles with high-dimensional problems common in computer systems. To overcome this limitation, we propose leveraging structured priors via Gaussian Processes to create Structured Bayesian Optimization (SBO). We introduce a novel framework that models the configuration space as a structured grid, capturing correlations among parameters to enhance search efficiency. We demonstrate the effectiveness of SBO on two real-world benchmarks: the NAS Parallel Synthetic benchmark and the Linux kernel TCP stack. Results indicate that SBO achieves superior performance compared to state-of-the-art techniques, requiring fewer than half the number of evaluations to locate the optimal configuration.

We present a new geometric model for heavy ion collisions that incorporates both the positions of individual nucleons and the collective motion of nucleon clusters. Within this framework, the impact parameter is expressed through the distance between collision centers and the impact nucleon number, while the anisotropy of initial spatial distributions is quantified by the multipole order. Our analysis indicates that the model successfully reproduces the centrality-dependent triangular flow ($v_3$) and the slope of the single-particle momentum spectrum, known as the HBT radius slope ($R_{\rm slope}$), across various collision systems including pp, pPb, and PbPb. Furthermore, the model allows for the estimation of initial multipole coefficients ($v_n$) and their corresponding harmonic components ($v_n^2$) from experimental data.

Linked Data has emerged as a transformative approach to organizing and sharing information across the web, enabling numerous innovative applications. However, the effectiveness of these uses is heavily contingent upon the high quality of the data involved. Unfortunately, the vast majority of Linked Data resources suffer from poor standards, which significantly hampers the adoption of Linked Data technologies. This paper introduces a crowdsourcing framework designed to enhance Linked Data quality by leveraging the collective efforts of multiple contributors. We specifically address the challenge of maintaining data consistency when different agents update their own data independently. To achieve this, we propose a novel versioning system that manages data versions and offers mechanisms for resolving conflicts between updates. Furthermore, we present a new algorithm that determines the optimal data quality by aggregating updates from various sources while accommodating user-defined preferences regarding data sources.

In the statistical analysis of stochastic processes, maximum likelihood estimation is frequently employed, yet it often yields biased results and suffers from inefficiency. To address these shortcomings, we propose a novel class of estimators based on score matching, which encompasses both unbiased and efficient solutions. We demonstrate the applicability of these methods through various illustrative examples.

We present new optical spectroscopy for the Seyfert galaxy NGC 4151, obtained with the Keck II telescope's Low Resolution Long-slit Spectrograph (LRLS) and the Keck I 10-m telescope's Double Spectrograph (DS). Our analysis reveals that the observed electron temperatures in NGC 4151 are significantly lower than those predicted by standard accretion disk models. Furthermore, our data indicate that the electron temperature varies across the spectrum, with higher values found at lower wavelengths. We propose that this variation arises from a combination of factors: the presence of a broad, low-density ionization cone, the influence of the stellar population, and the effects of dust scattering.

The rapid expansion of the Internet of Things (IoT) has created a growing demand for embedded applications capable of interacting with diverse IoT devices. Consequently, software vendors must ensure the reliability of IoT applications across a wide array of hardware, yet this task is significantly complicated by the vast diversity of IoT devices and the inherent limitations of embedded systems. This paper introduces a novel framework designed to automate the testing of IoT applications on multiple devices. The proposed approach employs a modular architecture that separates testing concerns, specifically isolating hardware interactions from the core test logic. By utilizing an abstract hardware interface, the framework allows test cases to remain hardware-agnostic, thereby streamlining the adaptation process for new devices. Furthermore, the system offers a modular hardware interface that simplifies the translation of abstract test cases into device-specific instructions. Experimental results indicate that this framework effectively reduces the time required to port test cases to new hardware, with the effort needed for adaptation varying based on the complexity of the test case.

The LHCb collaboration at CERN specializes in studying beauty and charm hadrons, with a key focus on CP violation and rare decays. This presentation reviews selected results from LHCb regarding neutral $B$ meson CP violation, covering time-dependent measurements of $B^0 \to J/\psi K_S^0$, $B^0 \to \phi K_S^0$, and $B^0 \to K^{*0} \bar{K}^{*0}$, as well as CP asymmetries in charged $B$ decays such as $B^\pm \to K^\pm \pi^0$, $B^\pm \to K^\pm \gamma$, and $B^\pm \to D K^\pm$.

Additionally, this talk covers results concerning CP properties of rare decays, specifically $B^0 \to \mu^+ \mu^-$ and $B^0_s \to \mu^+ \mu^-$. It also addresses the search for the rare mode $B^0 \to \pi^0 \nu \bar{\nu}$ and the determination of the CKM angle $\gamma$ through exclusive $B$ decays.

Realistic synthetic data is essential for training and evaluating autonomous driving systems. However, current traffic scene generation techniques often fail to accurately replicate genuine traffic dynamics, a shortcoming that hinders the creation of high-fidelity simulations. This paper introduces a novel, differentiable approach to generating realistic traffic scenes by modeling the underlying dynamics of real-world traffic. By modeling the latent distribution of these dynamics, our method employs a latent variable framework where the latent variable encodes the scene's generative structure. Using a variational autoencoder (VAE), we learn to sample diverse scenes from this distribution. Crucially, our model incorporates a novel latent interaction module that captures the complex, non-linear interactions among vehicles. Experiments demonstrate that our method successfully generates diverse, realistic traffic scenarios by manipulating latent variables, offering a powerful new approach for generating synthetic data for autonomous driving research.

We examine the Ising model within a Cayley tree context, specifically focusing on weakly periodic measures associated with normal subgroups of index 2. Our findings indicate that for any such measure, there exists a corresponding weakly periodic measure linked to a specific Bernoulli measure on a finite set of spins. This new measure exhibits invariance under a subgroup of index 16 derived from the original tree's automorphism group.

Developing numerical schemes for time-dependent partial differential equations requires balancing accuracy, efficiency, and stability. This paper introduces a new implicit scheme that is second-order accurate in both time and space, utilizing a variable time-stepping approach. The method is applied to solve the linear advection equation, and its performance is evaluated through numerical experiments.

A set of integer sequences qualifies as jointly ergodic if, for any jointly ergodic probability measure-preserving system and any non-constant functions within it, the specific average involving sequential iterations of the transformation and the sequences converges to the product of the individual function averages. We establish several theorems demonstrating that certain collections of polynomially defined iterated functions maintain joint ergodicity. Additionally, we introduce a criterion for identifying when a set of such sequences is maximal with respect to the property of joint ergodicity.

We present a three-dimensional, time-dependent, radiation-hydrodynamic simulation of a low-metallicity superbubble ($Z = 0.02 Z_{\odot}$) generated by a single $100 M_{\odot}$ star. Our study examines how dust grains evolve within the bubble's interior and its surrounding interstellar medium, specifically analyzing grain destruction and growth mechanisms. We find that grain growth occurs at a rate of approximately $10^{-4} M_{\odot} pc^{-2} yr^{-1}$ throughout the bubble's early evolution. This growth is driven by the coalescence of grains in the dense, shocked regions created when the superbubble's interior shocks interact with the bubble walls. Additionally, we observe that dust destruction in the bubble's interior is significantly reduced in low-metallicity environments compared to higher ones.

This study introduces a novel approach to enhance the detection of distant targets in the far field for autonomous vehicles, addressing the limitations of existing methods that primarily focus on near-field scenarios. The proposed method utilizes a two-stage framework: the first stage employs a lightweight, high-speed detector to generate an initial set of proposals, while the second stage refines these proposals by employing a refined detector trained on a newly created dataset. This second-stage detector is designed to be invariant to changes in object scale and aspect ratio, enabling it to accurately identify far-field objects. Evaluation results demonstrate that this approach significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art methods specifically in detecting distant objects.

This study employs full-dimensional potential energy surfaces (PES) to conduct quasi-classical trajectory (QCT) simulations of the H + H₂ → H₂ + H reaction. We introduce a novel method for generating QCT data specifically for Ring Polymer Molecular Dynamics (RPMD) by incorporating initial conditions derived from a QCT calculation into the RPMD framework. The primary objective is to evaluate the accuracy of RPMD in predicting reactive scattering outcomes for this system. Our analysis reveals that while RPMD accurately reproduces total and rotational cross sections, it significantly underestimates reactive probabilities and fails to correctly model rotational state distributions. Additionally, we examine the influence of the initial PES sampling method on these outcomes.

Non-rigid registration is a key technology for analyzing anatomical changes in medical treatments, particularly for tracking organ motion and deformation. This study introduces a novel approach to registering dynamic 3D medical images by integrating two components: a dynamic image registration model and a time-varying shape representation model. The proposed variational framework minimizes an energy function that incorporates a similarity measure alongside constraints for rigid body motion and shape preservation. To resolve this optimization problem, we utilize a level-set method featuring a specifically designed evolution vector field. The effectiveness of this algorithm is validated through experiments on both synthetic data and real-world scenarios involving the liver and heart.

This study examines the energy-momentum tensor of a static, spherically symmetric spacetime, which is characterized by two conformal matter collineations. We further investigate the conditions required for the existence of conformal matter collineations of higher orders. Our findings indicate that for a non-degenerate energy-momentum tensor, there is an absolute upper limit of two independent conformal matter collineations within this spacetime geometry. Additionally, we derive the specific forms of higher-order conformal matter collineations applicable to a degenerate, trace-free, and degenerate energy-momentum tensor.

Accurately determining motion vectors for points on dynamic 3D surfaces is vital for applications like robotic navigation and virtual reality. This paper introduces a novel, computationally efficient method for estimating motion in 3D space by leveraging the epipolar constraint and the structure from motion framework. Our approach utilizes two consecutive stereo image pairs from a dynamic scene, along with the corresponding 3D reconstruction of the first frame, to derive the motion vectors of the second frame. Specifically, we derive a closed-form solution for the updated stereo correspondence by incorporating the optical flow of the first frame and the 3D geometry of the first frame into the stereo constraint. Furthermore, we integrate the optical flow of the first frame into the stereo constraint to derive a closed-form solution for the motion vectors of the second frame. Although Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs) have achieved remarkable success in various domains, their high computational demands and memory usage often hinder their deployment on edge devices. To address these limitations, this study explores the application of Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) for classifying chest X-rays. We introduce a novel framework that converts convolutional ANNs into temporally sparse SNNs by converting their outputs into spike trains, allowing the conversion to occur directly on the original data without the need for retraining. Our results indicate that this approach enables the creation of highly accurate SNNs for medical image classification tasks, such as diagnosing pneumonia from chest radiographs, while significantly reducing energy consumption.

We have examined the thermodynamic properties of spin-polarized strange quark matter at finite temperature within a dense external magnetic field, utilizing the MIT bag model. By applying the one-loop perturbative QCD framework alongside the MIT bag model, we have derived the equation of state for such matter under these specific conditions. Our findings indicate that both the critical temperature and the critical density for the phase transition between spin-polarized strange quark matter and hadrons increase with the strength of the applied magnetic field. Furthermore, we have investigated how the radius of spin-polarized strange quark matter star varies with temperature and external field strength, observing that the radius diminishes as either temperature or the magnetic field strength increases.

A graph $G$ possesses the Perfect-Matching-Hamiltonian (PMH) property if every one of its perfect matchings can be paired with another perfect matching such that their union forms a Hamiltonian cycle. This paper demonstrates that the square of any tree with an even number of vertices exhibits the PMH-property.

The aim of this paper is to challenge the Bunyakovsky Conjecture, which suggests that any irreducible quadratic polynomial with integer coefficients that never yields values sharing a common factor greater than 1 with its input, should generate an infinite sequence of prime numbers. We demonstrate that this conjecture is false by providing a specific quadratic polynomial $P(n)$ that satisfies all specified conditions yet generates only a finite number of primes.

System call filtering serves as a vital security measure for containerized microservices, yet it remains difficult to implement effectively. Static analysis approaches often yield imprecise results because the dynamic nature of application behavior generates a vast array of potential execution paths, whereas dynamic analysis requires extensive testing to capture rare but significant calls. To address these challenges, we introduce Timeloops, a novel technique that leverages the inherent timing variability of applications to automatically identify system calls. By analyzing the timing patterns of API responses, Timeloops distinguishes between those that are consistently triggered and those that are sporadic, thereby isolating the necessary calls for security filtering. We evaluated this approach against both dynamic and static filtering methods using a diverse set of nine popular microservices applications. Timeloops successfully filtered 94% of system calls, outperforming dynamic methods by 1.9× and static methods by 2.1× in accuracy. Furthermore, it reduced filtering overhead by 94% compared to dynamic approaches and by 69% relative to static approaches.

We examine the spontaneous breaking of lepton number symmetry within the Standard Model, focusing on mechanisms that account for minimal neutrino masses through the generation of a majoron via right-handed neutrinos. Our study employs a majoron effective field theory to categorize possible interactions among Standard Model particles, majorons, and right-handed neutrinos. Furthermore, we analyze the implications of current experimental data on the majoron's coupling strengths and the masses of these right-handed neutrinos.

This study introduces a Poisson multi-Bernoulli mixture (PMBM) filter utilizing a grid-based intensity representation, offering a computationally efficient alternative to the Gaussian mixture (GM) intensity approximation typically found in existing methods. By employing a Rao-Blackwellized formulation, the proposed approach maintains the inherent strengths of the underlying multi-Bernoulli mixture (MBM) framework, specifically its capacity to handle targets with varying probabilities of existence and motion models without sacrificing these advantages. Crucially, this grid-based method yields a significant reduction in computational complexity compared to conventional Gaussian mixture approaches. A key benefit is the ability to perform data association using the exact likelihood function, thereby avoiding the approximations inherent in GM-based association. Simulation outcomes demonstrate that this technique not only matches the performance of the standard GM-PMBM filter but also surpasses it in both accuracy and efficiency.

This paper investigates the null controllability within a population dynamics framework featuring distributed delays in both death rates and population density measurements at death, specifically analyzing the impact of these delays on system controlability. By deriving new Carleman estimates, we establish the existence of distributed delay parameters that enable null controllability for the primary model and variants involving distributed death delays. Furthermore, we introduce several supplementary system variations, including undistributed delay scenarios, singular coefficients, and invertible operator relations, proving that null controllability persists in these cases through the application of previously established Carleman inequalities.

This study examines the optimal decision-making process in soccer during pivotal moments, such as penalty kicks or one-on-one defensive scenarios. By modeling these situations as a Markov Decision Process (MDP), we formulate the problem of selecting the best action. Specifically focusing on a goalkeeper deciding whether to dive or remain stationary during a penalty kick, we derive an analytical solution for the optimal strategy. Our approach determines the ideal reaction to a shooter's chosen direction by evaluating the expected goal probability for each possible action across all potential kick locations. Furthermore, we formulate the problem of choosing between diving and staying put as a comparison of expected goal probabilities, utilizing this framework to calculate the specific boundary that separates the conditions favoring a dive from those favoring no movement.

Full waveform inversion (FWI) has become a primary technique for imaging subsurface structures in seismic exploration by minimizing the discrepancy between recorded and synthetic wavefields. However, the computational expense of evaluating synthetic wavefields limits its application. Wavefield reconstruction inversion (WRI) addresses this by reconstructing synthetic wavefields using only forward operators, thereby reducing computational costs. A significant hurdle in WRI is the mismatch between the spatial and temporal resolutions of measured and reconstructed wavefields, which can degrade minimization accuracy. To resolve this, we propose a novel approach that incorporates a measured wavefield into the reconstruction objective function. This method ensures the objective function depends solely on the measured wavefield and maintains consistency with the true synthetic wavefield. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this new objective function is mathematically equivalent to the traditional WRI formulation. Numerical experiments confirm that this approach yields superior results compared to standard WRI methods.

We present an approach to achieve optical nonreciprocity within resonator modes by utilizing quantum squeezing. Our analysis demonstrates that the effects of Sagnac rotation and parametric pumping can be treated independently, allowing us to derive a unified Hamiltonian for a single-mode cavity that incorporates both. We then identify the conditions under which reciprocity breaks down at the level of individual modes, even when the cavity is far detuned from resonance. Our results indicate that the required degree of quantum squeezing needed to achieve this nonreciprocity is inversely proportional to the detuning. Furthermore, we show that this mechanism can be implemented in superconducting circuits.

We report the detection of coherent X-ray pulsations from the compact object in the eccentric binary system PSR J1929−2917, utilizing NuSTAR data collected on 2019 February 11. Our analysis reveals a spin period of $P = 1.11311(1)$ s, corresponding to a spin-down rate of $\dot{P} = 1.1(1) \times 10^{-17}$ s s$^{-1}$. The observed X-ray emission is phase-locked to the system's periastron passage, occurring at orbital phase $\phi_{orb} = 0.5$. This finding aligns with recent radio timing results indicating that the radio emission peaks near periastron, while our findings contrast with the behavior of the optical counterpart, which peaks at quadrature. Furthermore, the system's periastron advance is measured at $\dot{\omega} = 0.011(1)$ deg d$^{-1}$.

This study examines a reaction-diffusion prey-predator model incorporating immigration and emigration, incorporating a Holling type II functional response. We derive an implicit equation for the positive steady states and utilize it to investigate the global dynamics of the system. Specifically, we analyze the stability of these steady states and determine bifurcations, with a particular focus on Hopf bifurcations. Furthermore, we explore the implications of immigration and emigration parameters on species competition and coexistence.

The observation of the Sun's diurnal trajectory was fundamental to classical Islamic society, serving as the basis for regulating prayer times, determining fasting and Ramadan dates, and establishing civil and religious schedules. This study introduces a new, high-resolution dataset of Sun positions derived from diverse classical Islamic astronomical sources. We introduce "Azimuth Altitude" (AA) coordinates, a two-dimensional system designed to standardize astronomical records from various eras and geographies. By reconstructing daily solar paths from these normalized data points, we generate visual representations of the solar arc for specific cities and times. Furthermore, we propose a digital database to make this extensive corpus of astronomical data accessible to researchers.

This study examines a device-to-device (D2D) communication system where a data-holding D2D user leverages an intelligent reflecting surface (IRS) to enhance its link quality by reflecting signals toward a base station (BS) for data transmission. The optimization objective is to maximize the throughput of the D2D user by configuring the IRS passivity. To address this challenge, the work proposes a two-stage algorithm. Initially, the continuous phase shifts are optimized using a WMMSE framework, which incorporates a WMMSE-based precoder and decoders for the BS along with power control settings. Subsequently, the discrete phase shifts are refined based on the outcomes from the first stage. Simulation outcomes demonstrate that the suggested method outperforms traditional random phase allocation strategies.

This work introduces a novel methodology for Two-Dimensional (2D) Laser Doppler Vibrometry (LDV), designed to analyze the dynamic response of samples to stimuli. The proposed approach utilizes a single LDV sensor and a robotic arm to execute a scanning trajectory, with scanning parameters determined by a 2D grid-based search. This grid is established through a preliminary 1D LDV scan, which identifies the spatial locations of resonant frequencies. By integrating this technique with a 3D reconstruction algorithm, the system achieves full 3D mapping of vibration modes. Experimental validation was conducted on a guitar, demonstrating the method's capability to reconstruct 3D vibration patterns and accurately measure the corresponding frequencies.

We propose the use of programmable electrostatic phase plates to correct spherical aberration in Transmission Electron Microscopes, potentially enabling a spatial resolution of 0.08 nm. This approach involves a microelectrode array designed to generate a specific, non-periodic potential pattern that counteracts spherical aberration. The resulting image contrast is simulated using a model of a single atom, specifically a silicon atom, to demonstrate the method's viability.

Predicting suitable responses in dialogue is fundamental to the success of dialogue agents, yet the difficulty of anticipating the next utterance often stems from the difficulty of anticipating the subsequent dialogue state. We introduce a new end-to-end neural architecture that incorporates a hierarchical bidirectional LSTM to predict upcoming responses directly from the dialogue history. This architecture learns a representation of the dialogue state implicitly, thereby eliminating the need for explicit dialogue state tracking. Our approach was evaluated on the MultiWOZ dataset, a widely used benchmark for open-domain task-oriented dialogues. Experimental results indicate that our method achieves a significant improvement over the current state-of-the-art, surpassing previous scores by 2.0 BLEU and 1.5 ROBERTA.

This study introduces a novel deep learning framework designed for 3D LiDAR-based place recognition in autonomous driving, utilizing a shared convolutional architecture to process both raw point clouds and their corresponding 2D projections. By employing two separate convolutional layers for each data type, the system extracts hierarchical scene features, which are then fused via a fully connected layer to generate a unified place descriptor. This model is trained using a contrastive loss function. Experimental results on the large-scale S3DIS dataset demonstrate that this proposed method significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art approaches.

Cloud video transcoding represents a vital yet computationally demanding operation, necessitating significant processing power and memory. This study evaluates the performance of Java-based and FFmpeg implementations for video transcoding across various cloud virtual machine (VM) types, specifically examining how video format, resolution, and frame rate impact processing times. Leveraging these findings, the paper proposes a performance prediction model designed to optimize video transcoding workflows on cloud infrastructure. The study reveals that FFmpeg consistently outperforms Java across all tested scenarios, with performance gains ranging from 1.5 to 10 times depending on the specific video attributes. Furthermore, the research indicates that transcoding performance is highly sensitive to video characteristics, with frame rate exerting the most substantial influence. Finally, the proposed prediction model demonstrates strong accuracy, achieving a Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE) of approximately 10%.

We examine a system of massless Dirac fermions interacting via a repulsive Coulomb potential within graphene at non-zero densities within the mean-field approximation. At low temperatures, our findings indicate that the system exhibits a Mott-like insulating state characterized by a linear density-dependent gap. We further analyze the temperature dependence of this gap and the thermodynamic properties of the system. Our results show that the specific heat of the gapless (or effectively gaped) system of interacting Dirac fermions scales linearly with temperature at low T, implying the absence of a true quantum critical point separating this gaped phase from the semi-metallic phase.

This work also presents the first evaluation of models for paragraph-level Speech Text Generation (STG). This study derives explicit formulas for the Hessian matrix entries associated with the energy functional constrained by mass and charge, specifically for solitary wave solutions of the Klein-Gordon equation within a constant electric field. These results are then utilized to establish spectral stability criteria for solitary waves of specific types. Additionally, we identify a family of two-dimensional solitary waves where the Hessian matrix is indefinite, thereby proving the existence of unstable spectral points.

We investigate the dynamics of scalar field theories featuring both cubic and quartic interactions, focusing on the properties of Q-balls and the specific conditions required for their formation. Our analysis demonstrates that cores of Q-balls composed of these interactions must consist of the pure cubic component, while their surrounding envelopes are mixtures of both interaction types. Furthermore, we derive the necessary conditions for the existence of energetically stable, cored Q-balls. Finally, we compare our theoretical findings with numerical simulations of scalar field collapse to illustrate how these theories generate stable, cored Q-ball configurations.

We investigate the evolution of a cyclic cosmological model within a holographic framework by employing infrared cutoffs based on both the future event horizon and the Hubble radius. Our findings indicate that, regardless of the specific cutoff selected, the cyclic model fails to cyclically evolve within the viable parameter space required for holographic dark energy. Furthermore, when specifically utilizing the Hubble radius as the infrared cutoff, the cyclic cosmological model is incompatible with the cyclic nature of a cyclic universe within the context of holographic dark energy.

We introduce a novel invariant for graphs known as the bond scattering matrix, defined by the graph's Laplacian and a specified set of real, positive energies. This matrix serves as a powerful tool for distinguishing graphs that share identical bond invariants, thereby enhancing graph isomorphism detection. Furthermore, we demonstrate that graphs possessing the same bond invariant yield isospectral Laplacians, establishing the matrix as a refinement of the standard spectral invariant.

This paper examines the ring of integers within the rational group algebra $\mathbb{Q}[G]$ for a Galois extension $K$ with Galois group isomorphic to $A_5$, $S_4$, or $A_5$, specifically determining conditions where this ring is free over its corresponding Hermite normal form.

The Belle II experiment, utilizing the SuperKEKB collider, is currently in its data collection phase. This facility offers a unique opportunity to search for axion-like particles (ALPs) via the rare decay $B^+ \to K^+ E_i$, where $E_i$ represents either a photon pair or two photons. This search focuses on decays mediated by the coupling $B^+ \to K^+ E_i \to K^+ c\bar{u}$. By analyzing $740\,\text{fb}^{-1}$ of data, Belle II projects a sensitivity to detect $B^+ \to K^+ E_i \to B^+ \to K^+ \to B^+ \to K^+ \to B^+ \to K^+ \to B^+ \to K^+ \to B^+ \to K^+ \to B^+ \to K^+ \to B^+ \to K^+ \to B^+ \to K^+ \to B^+ \to K^+ \to B^+ \to K^+ \to B^+ \to K^+ \to B^+ \to K^+ \to B^+ \to K^+ \to B^+ \to K^+ \to B^+ \to K^+ \to B^+ \to K^+ \to B^

We introduce a new methodology for identifying diachronic semantic change that capitalizes on the strengths of contextualized embedding techniques while sidestepping their typical constraints. Our approach utilizes a contrastive learning framework to train a set of invariant semantic representations specifically sensitive to temporal shifts. We offer a novel algorithm to extract semantic change signals from these vector-based representations. Empirical evaluations across multiple datasets demonstrate that this method surpasses contemporary state-of-the-art approaches in both pinpointing instances of change and characterizing the direction of semantic movement.

The mass and spin of black holes in Active Galactic Nuclei (AGN) can be deduced from their electromagnetic spectra, with X-ray emissions serving as a particularly valuable diagnostic tool. This study presents a novel method for estimating spin and mass by analyzing the power density spectrum (PDS) of X-ray light curves. We developed a model that attributes the broad-band X-ray variability in AGN to fluctuations in the accretion disk's inner region, where the disk spectrum is generated via thermal Comptonization. In this framework, the characteristic timescales observed in the PDS correspond to the thermal and viscous timescales of the disk's innermost zones. We demonstrate that the relative magnitudes of these timescales are governed by the black hole's spin and disk viscosity, allowing the spin to be determined by analyzing the ratios of characteristic frequencies in the PDS. Furthermore, the absolute values of these frequencies depend on the disk's innermost radius, which is a function of both spin and mass; thus, the mass can be inferred by measuring the absolute frequency values. This methodology is tested using X-ray data from the Seyfert galaxy MCG-6-30-15, where we successfully recover spin and mass estimates consistent with those derived from previous X-ray spectral analyses.

Interkinetic nuclear migration (IKNM) is a fundamental process in brain development, characterized by nuclei moving along the apical-basal axis of the neuroepithelium in synchrony with cell division cycles. Although the significance of the cytoskeleton in this mechanism is well-established, the specific roles of individual components remain unclear. This study utilizes live imaging of *Xenopus* neuroepithelium to investigate interkinetic nuclear migration (IKNM) in relation to the distribution of the formin Diaphanous-related formin 2 (DFN2) and its partner, the spectraplakin adducin-2 (ADN2). Our findings reveal that DFN2 localizes to the basal cortex of the neuroepithelium in a division-cycle-dependent manner, accumulating at the basal membrane just prior to cytokinesis. Furthermore, the DFN2 isoform lacking an actin-binding domain (DFN2ΔABD) also exhibits this basal enrichment. In contrast, adducin-2 (ADN2) localizes to the apical cortex throughout the cycle. We demonstrate that the dynamic, cycle-dependent relocalization of DFN2 to the basal membrane is essential for proper IKNM. Mechanistically, we show that DFN2 recruits the actin depolymerizing factor cofilin to the basal cortex, and this recruitment is strictly required for correct nuclear migration.

This study introduces a new class of structured sparse matrices, termed $\mathcal{L}_0$-matrices, which are shown to be universal for recovering signals from undersampled data. We demonstrate that various practical coding schemes in image processing applications, such as video compressed sensing and color image demosaicing, inherently possess these $\mathcal{L}_0$-matrix characteristics. These codes are constructed from simple, deterministic patterns that exhibit low dimensionality in their undecorated forms. Furthermore, we propose recovery algorithms specifically designed for structured sparse matrices, which have been validated through simulations on both synthetic data and real-world scenarios.

This study examines the hydrodynamics of incompressible polar active fluids subjected to quenched disorder, where agents experience stochastic forces from randomly distributed, immobile obstacles. By employing a hydrodynamic coarse-graining approach, we derive the corresponding effective stochastic equations. Our analysis reveals that such fluids generally experience a disorder-induced drift velocity, which is proportional to the active force amplitude and inversely proportional to the alignment (polar) order parameter. This finding is supported by both analytical derivations and numerical simulations. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the collective motion of polar active matter can be harnessed to navigate through disordered environments, a capability that diminishes as alignment order increases.

This study presents a novel methodology for evaluating the security of communication networks within research institutions. The proposed approach utilizes a new simulation framework designed to assess the impact of Denial-of-Service (DoS) attacks on network connectivity. The simulation calculates the probability that a node becomes unreachable due to DoS, using this metric to gauge the overall vulnerability of a research institution's communication infrastructure. The framework was applied to the networks of five such institutions, using real-world data regarding their topology and the distribution of nodes susceptible to DoS. Simulation results indicate that approximately 20% of nodes in these networks are vulnerable to DoS attacks. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that the proposed simulation model aligns well with empirical data derived from active vulnerability scans.

We introduce a novel class of singularities in the electronic density of states, termed the "exceptional" vH singularity. This phenomenon occurs in strongly interacting electron systems where the conventional one-to-one correspondence between the Fermi level crossings and the Fermi surface breaks down due to the multi-valued nature of the latter. In specific two-dimensional systems, this singularity is flanked by conventional vH singularities and marks a transition from a hole-like to an electron-like Fermi surface. Its distinctive feature is a characteristic divergence in the sign of the associated spectral weight, a trait that emerges from the interplay between multiple vH singularities and the renormalized dispersion. This theoretical framework is substantiated by photoemission data from the 2×1 reconstructed surface of Bi2Se3.

This paper details the design and initial results of the Spallation Neutron Source (SNS) Muon Monitor, a device dedicated to measuring cosmic-ray muons and their associated spallation neutrons. The system comprises two distinct components: the Forward Monitor, positioned to capture high-energy muons and neutrons exiting the target, and the Backward Monitor, intended to detect lower-energy particles behind the target. The design of the Backward Monitor was specifically refined to achieve a more precise understanding of the neutron flux originating from low-energy muons. Initial data from the Forward Monitor indicate that the device successfully detects neutrons from spallation events triggered by individual muons.

This study examines the following nonlocal biharmonic Choquard problem:
$$
\begin{cases}
\Delta^2 u + \frac{\lambda}{2}\int_{\mathbb{R}^4} \frac{|u|^2}{|x-y|^2}\,dy + |u|^{p-2}u = f(u) & \text{in } \mathbb{R}^4, \\
u \in \mathcal{D}^{2,2}(\mathbb{R}^4),
\end{cases}
$$
where $2 < p < 4$, $f(u)$ is a specific nonlinearity, and $\lambda > 0$. We demonstrate the existence of ground state solutions for this problem.

Space-based missions like TESS have significantly expanded the catalog of transiting exoplanets, yet the precise masses and densities of most remain unknown. To address this, we utilize radial velocity (RV) data from the HARPS-N instrument to conduct a statistical study of 1,000 TESS targets, selecting them based on the likelihood of hosting low-mass planets. Our analysis reveals that 100 of these stars are likely single stars, making them prime candidates for future searches for small, non-transiting exoplanets using RV techniques. Furthermore, we identify 100 systems containing at least one confirmed exoplanet, with 100 additional systems hosting candidates that require further follow-up. Finally, we demonstrate that combining TESS transit data with our derived RV measurements allows for the determination of physical parameters for a broader range of exoplanets than RV data alone.

We introduce a system designed to extract text from machine-readable zones (MRZ) on ID card images using Optical Character Recognition (OCR). Upon extracting the raw text, the system validates it by cross-referencing the character counts and checksums defined by ISO/IEC 7810 and ISO/IEC 10008 standards. This approach is implemented in Python and is available as an open-source project on GitHub.

We examine the quantum harmonic oscillator subjected to a time-dependent external force, deriving closed-form expressions for both the unitary evolution operator and the Heisenberg position and momentum operators. By applying this framework, we calculate the exact time-dependent partition function, the Euclidean propagator, and various physical quantities. Furthermore, we introduce a general method to determine the quantum harmonic oscillator's behavior under arbitrary time-dependent forces through the use of iterative techniques.

The rotation of small asteroids is significantly influenced by the Yarkovsky-O'Keefe-Radzievskii-Paddack (YORP) effect, which stems from the anisotropic thermal re-emission of sunlight. This paper introduces a novel analytical approach to model the YORP effect by decomposing an asteroid's shape into spherical harmonics. This method is applied to analyze the rotation dynamics of an elongated, triaxial asteroid, with results demonstrating strong agreement against established analytical and numerical models. Furthermore, this technique is employed to simulate the YORP evolution of asteroid (130) Koruna, with outcomes aligning closely with those from the Discrete Element Method (DEM).

This study examines the role of social media in political discourse, analyzing over 1.5 million Twitter posts from 2015 to 2016 regarding the 2016 US Presidential Election. By leveraging sentiment analysis and network theory, we investigated the network structures surrounding political discussions and compared them to non-political content. Our findings reveal that political conversations form a more polarized network characterized by distinct, highly partisan communities with limited cross-party engagement. Furthermore, political discourse exhibits greater negativity and a higher frequency of retweets relative to original content. These patterns indicate that political discussions on Twitter are not only polarized but also function as echo chambers, where users primarily interact with like-minded individuals. Such an environment likely exacerbates political division and negatively impacts democratic processes.

Let $S$ be a compact surface equipped with its group of orientation-preserving diffeomorphisms, denoted as $\operatorname{Diff}^+(S)$. This paper demonstrates that any subgroup consisting of homeomorphisms which map the surface to itself while keeping a specific smooth curve $C$ invariant—and ensuring the smoothness of $C$ changes smoothly under these transformations—is not Roelcke precompact within the broader group of all such boundary-fixing diffeomorphisms, $\operatorname{Diff}(S, C)$.

We present the Gaia-Enceladus-Nordic (GEN) sample, comprising 1,000 stars from the APOGEE survey selected to exhibit a wide range of metallicities and ages. We utilize the GEN sample to evaluate the performance of the GENEVA stellar evolution models, focusing on their ability to simultaneously reproduce observed stellar rotation periods, effective temperatures, and surface gravities. Our analysis reveals that while the models successfully match the distributions of these properties for metal-rich ([Fe/H] > 0.0 dex) stars, they fail to do so for metal-poor ([Fe/H] < -0.5 dex) populations. Specifically, the models predict that ancient, metal-deficient stars rotate significantly faster than what is actually observed. We further demonstrate that this discrepancy persists even when accounting for stellar activity corrections and variations in the detection efficiency of Gaia. Given that precise stellar characteristics are fundamental to both stellar astrophysics and exoplanetary science, we conclude that future GENEVA model refinements must specifically address the rotation-age-age-metallicity relations for these low-metallicity stars.

We introduce line waves emerging at the interface of dual electromagnetic metasurfaces, a novel phenomenon distinct from conventional surface waves. These line waves are confined simultaneously within a specific plane and along a single axis perpendicular to that plane, resulting in confinement that is one-dimensional rather than two-dimensional. This phenomenon is achieved by employing a metasurface pair where one surface supports bound states in the form of surface waves, while the opposing surface generates a repulsive interaction. The resulting line waves exhibit tunable propagation constants and effective negative refractive indices. Furthermore, their spatial confinement dimensions can be adjusted through the selection of surface impedance parameters for both metasurfaces.

We introduce a novel framework for analyzing the enumerative complexity of conjunctive queries, with a specific focus on self-joins. Our approach employs a new class of automata known as $\mathcal{A}^{\text{list}}$-automata, which are designed to simulate the execution of a query. We demonstrate that the time required to enumerate answers to a query $Q$ using our proposed enumeration algorithm is bounded by $f(|Q|) \cdot T_{opt}(Q)$, where $T_{opt}(opt)$ represents the optimal evaluation time and $f(|Q|)$ is a function dependent on the query's size. Furthermore, we establish a matching lower bound for any deterministic algorithm operating within our model. Collectively, these findings indicate that our framework offers a tight characterization of enumeration complexity for self-join-heavy conjunctive queries.

Regular mappings between the hyperspaces of compact subsets of metric spaces are shown to be computable if and only if they are continuous. This finding is derived from the fact that the characteristic function of a regular function $f$, defined on $K(X)$, is equivalent in both directions to the continuity of $f$. This result extends prior work by Brattka and Sanchis regarding the continuity of set membership characteristic functions.

Using 3.0 inverse femtobarns of $ppbar$ collision data collected by the LHCb experiment at $\sqrt{s}=7$ TeV, we perform an amplitude analysis of the $B^0\rightarrow K^{*0}\overline{K}^{*0}$ decay. This analysis yields a branching fraction of $(4.4\pm0.5\pm0.4)\times10^{-7}$, normalized to the $B^0\rightarrow D^{-}D^{*+}$ decay, with total relative uncertainty of 11%. Additionally, we measure the longitudinal polarization fraction for the $B^0\rightarrow K^{*0}\overline{K}^{*0}$ decay as $f_L=0.65\pm0.08\pm0.04$, where the first uncertainty is statistical and the second is systematic.

Reservoir computing (RC) has emerged as a powerful tool for addressing complex dynamical system challenges, including time series forecasting and signal processing. Next-generation RC (NG-RC) represents a significant advancement over traditional RC by utilizing natural, unstructured reservoirs composed of random matrices or graphs. These systems require no training of internal connections, as they are inherently random, allowing the readout layer to be the sole component optimized for specific tasks. This study focuses on predicting chaotic time series using a next-generation RC framework built upon a random map that exhibits chaotic behavior. We demonstrate that next-generation RC can be trained with significantly less data than traditional RC, achieving superior forecasting accuracy with higher precision. Furthermore, we show that the system's ability to predict chaotic time series is directly linked to its ability to effectively learn from data.

A bias-reduced estimator for the population's median is proposed, specifically designed to enhance the performance of the standard linear mean regression model when applied to median analysis. By utilizing a bias-corrected approach, this estimator achieves a lower level of bias compared to the conventional method. The study includes simulation results that validate the effectiveness of this bias-reduced framework.

To address the computational inefficiency of current algorithms for solving variational Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs (HJI) equations, which hinders the tractability of differential games, we propose a novel algorithm that simultaneously resolves both the backward and forward problems. This method builds upon the established connection between variational Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs formulations and the deterministic control/estimation problems, offering a unified approach to handle them together.

We propose a novel multi-layer perceptron (MLP) architecture designed to learn signals by leveraging both global and local representations. This model integrates two complementary MLPs: one captures signal-wide features through a learned positional embedding, while the other focuses on localized details via learned attention mechanisms. This design offers a flexible, continuous representation that surpasses traditional discrete methods such as Fourier bases or voxel grids. Furthermore, it outperforms recent continuous architectures like NeuroRadiance Fields (NeRF) and 3D Gaussian Splatting. Our experiments demonstrate that these models achieve state-of-the-art results on both image and video benchmarks. Finally, we show that the dual-MLP structure excels in rendering speed, delivering a significant performance boost over NeRF.

Two competing theories attempt to account for the gradual progression of animacy representations found in the ventral temporal cortex: the functional segregation hypothesis, which posits distinct areas for animate and inanimate processing, and the functional continuity hypothesis, which suggests a continuous gradient of animacy coding. Previous research has struggled to differentiate between them, largely because it relied on binary classifications of stimuli that fail to capture naturalistic variation. To address this, we introduce an animate-ness continuum derived from deep neural networks, utilizing it to analyze functional MRI data from 1,000 participants. Our findings reveal that both hypotheses are supported by the data. Specifically, a continuous gradient of animacy encoding exists within the anterior temporal lobe, consistent with the continuity hypothesis. Simultaneously, a categorical distinction between animate and inanimate stimuli is observed in the lateral occipital and fusiform gyri, aligning with the segregation hypothesis. These complementary patterns suggest that animacy organization in the visual system is neither exclusively continuous nor strictly discrete, but rather a hybrid architecture combining continuous gradients with localized categorical hubs.

We establish a new bound for the count of Landau-Siegel zeros within a fixed family of Dirichlet $L$-functions, improving upon the result by Murty and Varma (1988). This enhancement is achieved by integrating our recent bound for the class number of imaginary quadratic fields with an innovative application of the large sieve method. Our approach yields an explicit inequality, $ \theta \leq 1 - \frac{0.0196}{\log D} $, where $\theta$ represents the Landau-Siegel zero associated with field discriminant $D$.

We introduce "qHRL," a novel logic for verifying relational quantum programs that incorporates expectations. This framework enables reasoning about both interference-sensitive security properties and standard performance metrics, such as runtime, within a unified approach. The core of qHRL is relational quantum Hoare logic, which extends classical relational logic with a fractional expectation variant. This extension allows fractional expectations to be distributed across multiple branches of quantum control flow. Furthermore, we define a relational expectation calculus specifically designed to support arithmetic and algebraic operations on these expectations. Finally, we present a sound method for simplifying expectations, ensuring that the complex relational expectations utilized in qHRL remain practical for real-world reasoning.

Super-spreader events, where a single individual infects a significantly larger number of contacts than the average, are recognized as a key factor in the rapid onset of epidemics. While the average number of infections per person ($R_0$) is typically treated as a constant, we demonstrate that when super-spreading occurs, the effective $R_0$ becomes a random variable. We propose a model in which the distribution of infections per person follows a negative binomial distribution, allowing us to derive an explicit formula for the distribution of the effective $R_0$. By applying this model to historical data from the 2009 H1N1 influenza pandemic, we show that the observed data aligns well with a negative binomial distribution. Furthermore, our findings indicate that the variance of the effective $R_0$ increases as the frequency of super-spreading events rises.

This paper offers new characterizations of codiskcyclicity for liftings of linear operators acting on a Hilbert space. It also establishes that the notion of codiskcyclicity generalizes both cyclicity and hyperbolicity.

We have created a new methodology to determine the magnetic field component perpendicular to the line-of-sight ($B_\perp$) using circular polarization ($V$) and linear polarization ($Q, U$) data from the ALMA observatory. This approach relies on the Faraday rotation of linear polarization and utilizes a single-layer Faraday screen model to fit the observed Stokes $V$ and $Q$ profiles. We demonstrate that this model yields a significantly more accurate $B_\perp$ estimate than the standard single-estimate Faraday depth ($\text{FD}_{est}$) technique, particularly when the Faraday distribution is broad. We further show that bias in the $\text{FD}_{est}$-derived $B_\perp$ measurement arises from the mismatch between the model and the true Faraday distribution, which is quantified by the bias in the estimated Faraday dispersion ($\sigma_{\text{bias}}$). By establishing a direct link between this bias and $\sigma_{\text{bias}}$, we can calculate the overestimated bias in $B_\perp$ using only the observed Stokes $I$, $Q$, and $V$ profiles, without requiring knowledge of the actual Faraday distribution. We also introduce a new bias-corrected $B_\perp$ estimator that incorporates the bias estimate. Validation against Monte Carlo simulations of the complete Faraday distribution indicates that this corrected estimator significantly reduces bias compared to the standard $\text{FD}_{

We present a new sample of 1,000 young star clusters in the Milky Way, identified through the Cluster Catalog of the Gaia Data Release 3. By analyzing the half-light radius and half-mass values for 1,000 of these clusters, we have established a mass-radius relationship applicable to the young cluster population. This relation reveals that as a cluster's mass increases, its effective radius also tends to grow. Furthermore, we examined the physical mechanisms governing the evolution of both mass and radius in such systems. Our findings indicate that while the initial mass and initial initial conditions are the primary drivers of radius evolution, the cluster's age plays a significant role in determining its final radius.

We present a QCD sum rule analysis of the $\eta_c \to \gamma\gamma$ process, specifically examining the dependence of the decay width on the charm quark mass. Our findings indicate that the hadron $\eta_c$ mass is not the appropriate parameter for this calculation; rather, the charm quark mass should be employed. Furthermore, our results align with the standard model prediction found in the Particle Data Group.

We introduce a novel determinant Monte Carlo approach for investigating finite-temperature correlation effects in doped Mott insulators, specifically within the two-dimensional t-J model. This method addresses the sign problem differently depending on occupancy: at half-filling, it circumvents the issue by utilizing determinant structures that mirror the exact low-energy $1/D$ expansion, whereas at doped levels, it employs a sign-reweighting technique with a significantly reduced magnitude of the sign problem. Our findings indicate that this new algorithm offers a substantial enhancement in efficiency compared to traditional Monte Carlo methods and related techniques, particularly for systems with doping far from half-filling.

We present a novel proof of the classical result stating that the Dickman function approximates the count of $y$-friable integers up to $x$ within a relative error of $O(x^{-\delta})$, where $\delta > 0$ is an arbitrarily small constant. Our approach relies on a fresh, self-contained derivation of the differential delay equation satisfied by the Dickman function, utilizing only the identity due to Dickman himself that expresses $F(y)=\int_{1}^{y} t^{-1} F(y/t)\,dt$. This new method bypasses earlier techniques which depended on intricate inequalities involving $F$ and required ad hoc arguments to establish the necessary error term.

We examine the complexity functions associated with a class of non-erasing morphisms on a free monoid $\sigma: A^* \to B^*$, alongside their image subshift $X = \sigma(B^*)$. Our analysis establishes that these functions are intimately connected, allowing us to utilize the complexity function of $X$ to characterize $\sigma$ within the closure of all such morphisms.

Current multi-task language models rely on a shared representation layer trained via task-specific labels, which limits their ability to generalize across new tasks. While recent approaches attempt to mitigate this by learning task-agnostic representations, they often fail to generalize effectively to unseen tasks. In this paper, we introduce a new framework designed to enhance cross-task generalization in multi-task settings. Our framework consists of two key components: a task-agnostic representation module and a task-adaptive module. The task-agnostic module captures representations useful for various tasks, whereas the task-adaptive module learns task-specific adjustments from task prompts. Experiments demonstrate that our framework significantly surpasses both standard multi-task models and recent prior approaches when evaluated on new tasks.

This study introduces a new algorithm called m-ar-K-FastICA for feature extraction, designed to enhance the original FastICA method. The proposed approach incorporates a modified symmetric function into the objective function to improve performance when processing random data. Additionally, the adaptive strategy employed in m-ar-K-FastICA allows for the automatic determination of the scaling parameter $s$, thereby enhancing the algorithm's adaptability. Comparative analyses using both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that m-ar-K-FastICA outperforms the standard FastICA method in terms of effectiveness.

This work examines the dynamics of the gaming market by analyzing data from Steam's sales tracking system. By applying advanced statistical methods, we evaluate the industry's structure, dynamics, and behavior. Our analysis reveals that the gaming sector functions as a complex system characterized by multifractality, long-term memory, and significant cross-correlations between product releases. Furthermore, the study highlights the strong influence of the "word-of-mouth" phenomenon on sales performance. These insights offer valuable perspectives for optimizing business strategies and enhancing decision-making processes within the industry.

We introduce a class of Gaussian Process-based hyperparameter tuning algorithms designed for differentially private stochastic gradient descent (DPSGD). These methods integrate into the existing DPSGD loop to facilitate efficient, private hyperparameter optimization. Our approach addresses the challenge of privately gathering private information by privately querying the system with various hyperparameter configurations. We demonstrate the method's efficacy through experiments on several datasets, showing that it successfully identifies high-performing private hyperparameters. Furthermore, we propose an innovative private acquisition function that leverages Gaussian Process regression to privately predict model outcomes based on their corresponding private information, thereby enhancing the quality of private information gathered during the process.

Let $(W,S)$ be a Coxeter system. The complex of boolean involutions, denoted $B_I(W,S)$, consists of all non-empty subsets $J \subseteq S$ such that the element $w_J := w_J$ is an involution. In this paper, we establish the homotopy type of $B_I(W,S)$ for any finite-dimensional type $(d)$: if $W$ has dimension $d$, then $B_I(W,S)$ is homotopy equivalent to a complex of dimension $\lfloor d/2 \rfloor$. This finding extends previous work by D. Davis and K. Liu, who demonstrated that the case where $d$ is even implies the complex is homotopy equivalent to a $(d-1)/2$-dimensional sphere.

Correlated noise in readout sequences significantly impacts the sensitivity of astronomical devices. This study introduces a method to measure correlated readout noise by analyzing the power spectral density of a single, uniform flat-field exposure. We validate this approach using data from the Subaru Hyper Suprime-Cam (HSC), specifically examining the 1.5-second readout mode. Our analysis reveals that noise correlations extend up to 10 readout frames, accounting for approximately 10% of the total variance. We further demonstrate that this noise limits the flux measurement precision for point sources to 0.5% for a magnitude of 20 and 0.05% for a magnitude of 15. Finally, we show that implementing a simple detrending algorithm can mitigate this correlated noise by a factor of 100.

We introduce a novel, semi-analytical framework designed to model the chemical evolution of galaxies, with a specific focus on the distinct contributions of supernovae types Ia and II to the enrichment of stellar elements. Our model incorporates the formation histories of both individual stars and stellar populations, alongside the delayed time distributions associated with supernova events. By leveraging this approach, we derive analytical expressions for the abundance ratios of specific elements—namely Fe, Ca, and Ni—as functions of stellar age, metallicity, and the time elapsed since a galaxy's formation. These expressions are subsequently utilized to construct predictive relations for [Fe/H] versus [Ca/Fe] and [Fe/H] versus [Ni/Fe] in the context of stellar populations. To account for stochastic variations in enrichment, we derive analytical formulas for the widths of chemical tagging distributions. Furthermore, we develop a semi-analytical method to estimate the likelihood of a star belonging to a specific halo substructure based on its elemental abundances. When compared against recent observational data from the Gaia-Enceladus and Sagittarius satellites, our model successfully reproduces the observed trends in mean abundances and the calculated tagging distribution widths.

During the COVID-19 pandemic, online misinformation spread rapidly across social media, often challenging official guidance and exacerbating public confusion. This study examines the propagation of such rumors on Weibo, utilizing a Susceptible-Infected-Susceptible (SIS) epidemic model adapted for complex networks. We analyze the system's steady states and their stability, deriving a novel threshold value that determines whether misinformation will eventually vanish or become endemic. Furthermore, we investigate control mechanisms by examining the impact of both proactive vaccination and reactive retweeting on rumor dynamics. Our findings offer significant implications for mitigating the spread of online falsehoods during future global crises.

Planetary Nebulae (PNe) serve as valuable tools for determining host galaxy distances via the Tully-Fisher relation, a method that relies on accurately measuring their line-of-sight velocities. This study presents a new technique for determining radial velocities using the Doppler shift of emission lines, specifically analyzing the [O III] $\lambda$5007 line. The approach involves fitting a Gaussian function to the line profile to extract velocity data. Using the Hubble Space Telescope's Advanced Camera for Surveys, we measured velocities for 100 PNe in the Andromeda Galaxy (M31). Our results indicate that the method achieves a precision of approximately 15 km s$^{-1}$ for individual planetary nebulae.

We introduce LifeStream, a streaming engine designed to handle physiological data. Although such data is abundant and valuable, existing specialized tools often lack the capacity to conduct thorough analyses. Conversely, traditional streaming processors are ill-suited for this domain due to rigid requirements like fixed schemas, high-velocity processing, and complex query languages that do not align with the characteristics of physiological information. Addressing these limitations, LifeStream offers a flexible, user-friendly, and safe environment for processing such data. It features a schema-less, type-safe data model that automatically infers types from JSON payloads, along with an expression-based API that mirrors the structure of Python code. Furthermore, the engine integrates with Jupyter notebooks to enable interactive analysis. Evaluation results indicate that LifeStream effectively processes diverse real-world physiological datasets while supporting both efficient and expressive queries.

This study investigates the existence of timelike (1,n)-Bertrand curves within the framework of Minkowski space $\mathbb{E}^ {1,n}$. Initially, we establish the necessary conditions defining these curves. Subsequently, we demonstrate that such curves exist only when $n=2$.

The selection of a loss function is a critical component in training deep neural networks for supervised classification. While numerous options exist, the field lacks a systematic method for evaluating and comparing them. This paper introduces a rigorous framework designed to assess and contrast various loss functions. The proposed approach involves three key stages: formally defining supervised classification and the concept of a loss function, analyzing the theoretical properties of specific losses, and finally, empirically comparing their performance. We illustrate this methodology by applying it to several deep convolutional architectures for image classification, focusing on cross-entropy, hinge, and exponential loss variants.

This study presents the design of a linear stabilizable boundary feedback controller for a class of Navier-Stokes equations defined on a rectangular domain, specifically addressing scenarios where the external force field is periodic in time. We establish the existence of a solution that ensures local exponential stability for these periodic systems. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this approach can be generalized to other domains exhibiting partial controllability when subjected to various periodic forcing functions.

Strain-induced crystallization (SIC) is a distinctive feature of certain unfilled polymers, where mechanical stretching triggers molecular alignment and the subsequent formation of crystalline structures. This phenomenon significantly alters both mechanical and thermal characteristics, thereby complicating the prediction of material behavior under varying conditions. This study introduces a novel thermodynamic framework that accounts for SIC within the context of finite elasticity theory. The proposed approach derives the Helmholtz free energy function by integrating contributions from amorphous and crystalline phases, incorporating a kinetic model to describe the evolution of crystallinity. The model is validated against experimental data for natural rubber, demonstrating its capability to accurately capture key phenomena, including the hysteresis loop in stress-strain responses, the reduction in Young's modulus, and the heat generation associated with SIC.

This study investigates the pairing symmetry of superconductivity in doped topological insulator Bi$_2$Se$_3$ by analyzing the temperature-dependent penetration depth, $\lambda(T)$, derived from microwave conductivity measurements. The results indicate that the observed superconductivity aligns with an $s$-wave symmetry, specifically a fully gapped $s_{\pm}$-wave state where the gap on the hole pocket is significantly larger than that on the electron pocket. Furthermore, the study finds that the magnitude of the London superfluid density remains largely unaffected by the strength of spin-orbit coupling.

A primary hurdle in Imitation Learning lies in securing high-quality teacher feedback, a situation exacerbated when the teacher's knowledge evolves over time. We introduce a novel Reinforcement Learning framework designed for teachers who provide feedback intermittently, enabling agents to master tasks with sparse guidance despite infrequent input. Our framework incorporates a learned task-agnostic reward function that offers dense, positive reinforcement whenever the teacher updates their feedback. By leveraging this approach, we enable agents to achieve expert-level performance with minimal direct interaction, while simultaneously encouraging frequent teacher updates through consistent reinforcement for every feedback revision.

Conventional non-coherent differential detection serves as a widely adopted method for Continuous Phase Modulation (CPM), valued for its simplicity and low hardware requirements. However, this method suffers from significant performance degradation in the presence of Doppler shifts. This study introduces a simple differential detection scheme designed to mitigate Doppler effects, which functions similarly to the conventional approach but incorporates a specific pre-detection filtering stage. The proposed technique is evaluated across various CPM schemes, including Minimum Shift Keying (MSK), Offset-MSK (O-MSK), and Gaussian MS (GMS), demonstrating that it achieves substantial performance gains. Furthermore, the paper derives an analytical expression for the bit error rate (BER) that aligns closely with simulation outcomes.

We present a three-dimensional core-collapse simulation of a 19.5 M\(_\odot\) progenitor star, utilizing the ENZO code. This simulation is employed to determine the binary formation outcomes of neutron star and black hole systems. The derived formation conditions are subsequently utilized to evaluate the merger rates of neutron star–black hole, neutron star–neutron star, and black hole–neutron star binaries. Our results indicate that the merger rate for the neutron star–black hole system is approximately 1.5 times higher than that predicted by conventional parametric models. Furthermore, the simulation suggests that the current non-observation of such mergers by LIGO/Virgo does not necessarily rule out core-collapse mechanisms for forming neutron stars and black holes, as the existing constraints may be influenced by the limited number of simulated events. Additionally, our findings imply that the currently unobserved gravitational wave signals from black hole–neutron star mergers could potentially be used to constrain the equation of state for neutron star matter.

We introduce a new density-dependent energy density variance, applicable to both thermal and non-thermal quantum systems, which quantifies fluctuations relative to the mean by incorporating the energy density itself. Utilizing this metric, we examine how the variance of energy density behaves in a free scalar field theory across different regimes of temperature and chemical potential. Our findings reveal that the variance of the energy density is a valuable probe for investigating phase transitions and the nature of matter in the early universe.

Deep learning-based image deraining techniques have achieved remarkable success, largely due to the availability of large-scale datasets containing synthetic rain. However, current research indicates that models trained on synthetic data struggle to effectively remove rain from real photographs. This discrepancy arises because existing datasets often fail to capture the complex diversity of actual rainfall, leading to a significant gap between training and testing conditions. To address this challenge, we introduce a new dataset comprising 10,000 high-quality real rainy images collected from the web. We propose a novel deraining framework that leverages the inherent diversity of these authentic rain samples. Specifically, our approach trains a domain-invariant network using a cycle-consistency loss to create a robust, domain-general model capable of handling various rain types. Furthermore, we introduce a multi-scale recurrent module designed to capture both local and global rain structures. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance on both synthetic and real benchmarks.

A prevalent technique for reward learning involves humans providing preference data, yet this approach is often prohibitively expensive and prone to errors. We introduce a new method that enables agents to learn rewards by querying humans with multiple options and asking for a single binary "yes/no" decision, thereby reducing the decision space from an infinite scale to just two. We demonstrate that this strategy is theoretically grounded, practically effective, and can achieve the same performance as traditional methods using significantly less data.

This paper addresses the question of whether a model companion exists for set theory under the assumption that the Continuum problem is undecidable. We demonstrate that if the continuum hypothesis is independent of ZFC, then ZFC lacks a model companion. Furthermore, we establish a broader result: if T is any consistent theory extending ZFC and the continuum problem is undecidable relative to T, then T also has no model companion.

In contrast, assuming the continuum hypothesis holds within ZFC, we construct a theory S that serves as the model companion for set theory. This companion theory S is characterized by specific axioms, including the assertion that the continuum is exactly $\aleph_1$, the principle of Dependent Choice, and the statement that every subset of $\aleph_1$ is constructible.
