" (Note: The original text had this as the first sentence of the second section; the paraphrase combines the two to maintain flow while summarizing the content across the entire two sections.)

This study examines the relationship between personality traits, drug consumption habits, and misuse by administering a questionnaire to 1,000 participants. The survey utilized the Big Five Inventory-2 (BFI-2) to assess personality, alongside the Drug Use Disorder Identification Test-Revised (DUDIT-R) and a consumption habits questionnaire. Data analysis via multiple linear regression revealed that Neuroticism, Extraversion, and Openness to Experience significantly predicted DUDIT-R scores, whereas Age, Gender, and Education Level were not significant predictors. These findings suggest that specific personality traits are key factors in understanding drug use patterns, with implications for targeted prevention and treatment strategies.

Current commonsense reasoning systems often rely on external knowledge sources, yet these resources typically prioritize semantic relationships over temporal dynamics. To address this gap, we introduce ATOMIC, a large-scale dataset containing 1.1 million short narratives that demand temporal commonsense reasoning. ATOMIC emphasizes temporal reasoning by organizing its knowledge through a temporal graph structure, where nodes represent events and edges denote temporal relations. This framework enables the encoding of intricate temporal scenarios and supports the generation of logical stories from simple premises. In contrast to existing approaches, our method for processing ATOMIC incorporates temporal reasoning specifically designed to handle these complex inter-event relationships. Comprehensive evaluations reveal that while current models perform adequately on simpler tasks, they significantly lag behind human performance when confronted with more advanced reasoning challenges within the dataset.

We demonstrate the application of a quantum algorithm for financial portfolio optimization by employing the HHL method. Our approach formulates the optimization problem as a linear system of equations, enabling the use of HHL to determine the optimal asset allocation. This framework facilitates the analysis of how quantum techniques can be integrated into financial engineering, with specific attention to the algorithm's performance characteristics and the design of appropriate quantum state loaders. Furthermore, we present a novel, simplified state preparation technique that reduces circuit complexity relative to existing methods, while maintaining the efficiency of the overall HHL implementation.

This paper introduces a novel framework designed to enhance data efficiency in end-to-end automatic speech recognition (ASR) through multimodal training. Although current end-to-end ASR models have achieved state-of-the-art results by integrating diverse acoustic and linguistic features, two significant hurdles remain: the necessity for massive data volumes and the high cost of training on multiple modalities. To address these issues, we propose a new architecture featuring a shared multimodal backbone and two distinct projection modules. This design enables the creation of two separate but functionally equivalent representations—one derived from fusing all modalities and another generated using only acoustic data. By aligning these representations, the model can effectively leverage information from both sources. Furthermore, we introduce a novel data selection strategy that identifies the most valuable samples for training. Experiments conducted on the VoxPopuli dataset demonstrate that this approach yields a 1000% improvement in data efficiency with only a negligible sacrifice in recognition accuracy compared to the baseline.

This study derives the average cross-sectional area of an arbitrary shape in $n$-dimensional Euclidean space, demonstrating that it equals $V_n/c_n$, where $V_n$ represents the shape's $n$-dimensional volume and $c_n$ is the average cross-sectional area of a unit $n$-dimensional ball. Furthermore, it is shown that this average cross section is maximized when the shape is centrally symmetric, with its maximum value being the average cross section of a shape having unit volume.

This study examines the random uniform parking function $f_n$ of length $n$ within the space $\{1,\dots,n\}^n$. As $n$ approaches infinity, the initial $k_n$ entries of $f_n$ are shown to behave as independent samples drawn from a specific distribution $\mu_{n}$ defined on $\{1,\dots,n\}$. Furthermore, an explicit closed-form expression for $\mu_{n}$ is provided.

We report on the observation of a DC conduction blockade in superconducting nanowires, which occurs at specific discrete values of the critical current. This blockade is eliminated by applying a small magnetic field parallel to the wire, while a minimal transverse magnetic field induces oscillatory behavior in the blocked current as the field strength increases. These phenomena are attributed to the formation of a single Josephson junction along the nanowire, resulting from a vortex pinning mechanism that creates a notched critical current profile. Consequently, these effects offer a novel pathway for utilizing superconducting nanowires in the development of DC quantum meters and superconducting single-photon detectors.

We present the results of a spectroscopic analysis of the spectrum of GJ 229B, the first exoplanet spectrum analyzed via full spectral retrieval. Utilizing the latest version of the open-source radiative transfer code, NEML3, we performed Bayesian spectral retrievals on the observed near-infrared spectrum (0.6–5.1 $\mu$m) obtained from the Keck II telescope. Our methodology integrates high-resolution spectra from multiple instruments, utilizing the NEML3 radiative transfer code to infer atmospheric properties via Bayesian inference. We employed the open-source Python package PyMC3 to implement the Bayesian inference, utilizing the ExoMol database for molecular opacity data. Our analysis reveals that the atmospheric structure of GJ 229B is highly degenerate, with the effective temperature ($T_{\rm eff}$) and surface pressure ($P_{\rm surf}$) exhibiting a strong anti-correlation. We examine the Bjorken scaling behavior of structure functions within a thermal environment, specifically analyzing the implications for the parton distribution function (PDF) in such a medium. We demonstrate that if the thermal parton density is sufficiently low, structure functions adhere to Bjorken scaling only if the thermal parton density is sufficiently low, implying that the PDF exhibits a dependence solely on the Bjorken variable $x$. Conversely, we show that at high densities, structure functions cannot satisfy Bjorken scaling regardless of the $x$-dependence of the medium's PDF. These conclusions are derived within the leading-logarithm approximation of perturbative QCD, utilizing the DGLAP evolution equation to describe the parton density function.

We introduce NovelView2Video, a method designed to generate novel view videos from a single image. Our approach leverages a recently developed dataset containing over 1 million novel view video pairs, featuring a maximum viewing angle of 90 degrees. To achieve this, we utilize a multi-stage framework that combines Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) with a specialized temporal upsampling technique. This combination enables the prediction of high-resolution, novel view videos with a viewing shift of up to 90 degrees based solely on a single input image.

Inter-orbital coupling, a phenomenon recently recognized as pivotal in advancing nanoscale optoelectronics, has been successfully demonstrated in a photonic lattice. This achievement was realized by integrating a silicon-on-insulator photonic crystal with a tunable graphene layer. The study reveals that this coupling arises from the tunable overlap between the evanescent fields of two distinct photonic modes: a high-energy H-like mode and a low-energy P-like mode. By adjusting the graphene's Fermi level, researchers can independently control the coupling strength and the relative energy levels of these modes. Furthermore, by varying the carrier density within the graphene, the system can be tuned to achieve a resonant condition where the H and P modes share identical energies. This mechanism enables the manipulation of the photonic band structure, specifically inducing a transition from a direct to an indirect bandgap. Consequently, this phenomenon facilitates the realization of tunable photonic Weyl points and allows for the control of photonic chiral edge states.

We examine the magnetic form factors of the $\Omega^-$ baryon, which consists of three strange quarks, by applying dispersion relations. These relations connect the imaginary parts of the form factors to their real parts through Hilbert transforms. The imaginary components are determined via optical theorem calculations involving the corresponding scattering cross-sections. Our findings indicate that the real parts of these form factors are sensitive to the energy dependence of the imaginary parts, allowing for a more precise determination of the real components. Furthermore, we observe that the real parts are significantly larger than those derived from previous models.

Air transmission of viruses via contaminated aerosols is influenced by complex interactions between fluid dynamics and mass transfer, which vary across different indoor environments. This study examines airflow patterns and the transport of virus-carrying aerosols within a typical examination room in China, utilizing Large Eddy Simulation (LES) coupled with a dynamic subgrid-scale model. The LES framework employs the Smagorovs-Lilly model to address airflow complexities, while the Contaminant Transport Model (CTM) utilizes a scalar subgrid model to simulate the distribution of virus-laden particles. The simulation setup incorporates realistic boundary conditions, including the specific geometry of the room, the layout of furniture, and the operational parameters of ventilation systems. Results indicate that airflow structures significantly dictate the spatial distribution of these aerosols. Specifically, the interaction between ventilation jets and recirculation zones formed by obstacles like desks and chairs creates distinct high-concentration areas. These findings offer valuable insights for optimizing indoor ventilation strategies to mitigate airborne infection risks.

We introduce the concept of birefringent scattering, wherein an x-ray beam traversing an intense laser field experiences differential refraction based on its polarization states. This phenomenon arises from the interaction between the x-rays and the ponderomotive forces generated by the laser, causing circularly polarized x-rays to refract differently than linearly polarized ones. Consequently, the scattering process induces a conversion from linear to circular polarization. We demonstrate that this birefringent scattering serves as a mechanism to amplify the laser's effect on electron dynamics, specifically enhancing circular dichroism in photoelectron emission. This increase in dichroism results in a more pronounced sensitivity to the combined circular polarizations of the laser and the x-ray pulse. Furthermore, we show that this effect enables the isolation of circularly polarized x-rays through scattering off a target, offering a method to generate high-intensity beams with circular polarization.

This study introduces the concept of fully transitive polyhedra, defined as those admitting a symmetry group that acts transitively on their flags. We demonstrate that every such polyhedron must be either Euclidean or hyperbolic. Additionally, we establish a novel class of hyperbolic fully transitive polyhedra by applying a hyperbolic generalization of the method used to construct regular semi-regular tilings through circle packings.

We introduce the concept of unclonable encryption, a framework designed to prevent adversaries from generating multiple ciphertexts that decrypt to the same message. In this model, an encryption scheme encrypts a message into several distinct components, where any two components are incompatible for decryption. We establish security definitions for both public-key and identity-based variants of unclonable encryption, demonstrating that our proposed schemes achieve security under the standard generic group assumption. Furthermore, we present an application of this encryption model to the creation of unclonable signatures.

This paper examines information-theoretic authentication at the physical layer for channels subject to an adversary who can intercept and alter transmissions. We demonstrate that if the channel exhibits a certain inherent property, an authenticator can be constructed; conversely, we provide a counterexample showing authentication is impossible when this property is absent. Our positive construction relies on a universal source-channel coding scheme, which we prove achieves both authentication and reliable communication with a rate matching the channel capacity. Notably, this construction remains effective even when the adversary possesses unlimited computational power and access to an arbitrary adversarial strategy.

We present a theoretical investigation into plasmon excitations within twisted bilayer transition metal dichalcogen (TMDC) layers, utilizing a tight-binding framework that incorporates both inter- and intralayer van der Waals interactions. Our analysis reveals that low-damped, quasi-flat plasmon modes emerge exclusively when the system exhibits flat electronic bands accompanied by strong interlayer coupling. Specifically, these modes are observed at low carrier densities and within a narrow frequency range, where their energy levels closely track those of the underlying flat bands. By varying the lattice constant, we demonstrate that these modes can be dynamically tuned across a wide spectrum. Furthermore, we show that these low-energy plasmons can be converted into high-energy variants through increased carrier density, a mechanism applicable to the development of tunable plasmonic devices.

This study examines the characterization of the potential function for an almost gradient nearly soliton on an almost Sasakian manifold, which is shown to be a real analytic function. Additionally, it is established that an almost soliton is real analytic if the potential function is almost Sasakian and the scalar curvature is constant. Lastly, it is demonstrated that the almost soliton is a real analytic gradient almost soliton if the potential function is almost Sasakian and the scalar curvature is constant.

The evolution of stars is governed by their mass loss, a process driven by different mechanisms in various stellar types: radiation pressure on spectral lines dominates in massive stars, whereas thermal pressure of coronal loops controls mass loss in lower-mass stars like the Sun. While our understanding of the former is relatively well-established, the drivers behind the latter remain poorly understood. This study presents a novel 3D MHD simulation of a coronal mass ejection (CME) triggered by magnetic reconnection within a magnetic flux rope. The model employs a newly developed, computationally efficient reconnection algorithm capable of handling strong magnetic fields. The simulation successfully reproduces key observational features of CMEs, including the formation of a magnetic flux rope, the acceleration of a CME-like structure, and the release of non-thermal particles. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that reconnection can trigger a "slingshot" effect, wherein a reconnected flux rope interacts with a residual magnetic field to accelerate outward. These findings offer a potential explanation for the observed high velocities of interplanetary CMEs.

Spin-Orbit Coupling (SOC) can be significantly amplified at a single atomic layer adjacent to a spin-orbit heavy element, a phenomenon known as proximity-induced SOC. This enhancement is governed by the specific electronic structure of the interface, particularly the hybridization between the surface states of the material and those of the heavy partner. In this study, we examine the SOC of the topmost atomic layer in MoS$_2$ when interfaced with WSe$_2$, employing Density Functional Theory (DFT) calculations. Our findings reveal that proximity-induced SOC in MoS$_2$ is governed by hybridization with specific bands in WSe$_2$, notably those derived from Mo d-states. Furthermore, we demonstrate that SOC can be further intensified by manipulating the interlayer twist angle, a factor that critically influences the character of the interface states.

This work presents bound state solutions for a fractional, one-dimensional double semi-relativistic Schrödinger equation featuring a modified Pöschl-Teller potential. Initially, we derive the general form of the potential and the corresponding fractional Schrödinger equation. Subsequently, we determine the energy eigenvalues and associated eigenfunctions by applying the factorization method. Finally, a fractional tunneling analysis is conducted across the potential barrier.

We introduce a methodology for incorporating constraints on the Lipschitz constants of specific parameters within a neural network into the training process. This approach is applicable to various architectures, including ResNets, VGGs, and others. We demonstrate that the network's Lipschitz constant can be expressed as the maximum value of a function defined over a compact domain, allowing this constraint to be integrated into stochastic gradient descent via mini-batch processing. Our experiments reveal that this technique enhances the generalization performance of models without compromising their accuracy.

Sequential neural network approaches have recently demonstrated success in predicting grammatical features across various languages, yet their efficacy varies significantly. This study specifically examines agreement prediction in Basque and English, revealing that while sequential models perform well for English, they struggle with Basque. We argue that this difficulty stems from the fact that Basque agreement is non-sequential in nature, relying instead on complex interactions between multiple word order positions. To address this, we propose a novel recurrent neural network architecture designed to capture non-sequential patterns within a sequence. By integrating this model, we achieve state-of-the-art performance on the Basque agreement task, surpassing previous results by 3.5%.

We investigate the atmospheric and surface conditions of exoplanets in highly eccentric orbits, utilizing a 1D General Circulation Model (GCM) to simulate the atmosphere of a K2-140b analog. This hypothetical exoplanet orbits a K7V star with a 100-day period and an eccentricity of 0.4, featuring a 1:1 spin-orbit resonance and a 10-bar H/He envelope. Our simulations reveal that eccentricity significantly alters the planet's thermal structure and atmospheric circulation. The orbital dynamics cause a 100\% variation in received stellar radiation, peaking at periastron, which drives a 100\% fluctuation in equilibrium temperature and shifts the peak wind speeds by approximately 100 m/s. Furthermore, the peak insolation at periastron induces a permanent day-night temperature differential of roughly 100 K. These findings highlight that eccentricity is a critical factor in determining the atmospheric and surface evolution of exoplanets.

Rehabilitation often demands repetitive movements that can be demotivating; modified digital games offer a potential solution by enhancing engagement. This study introduces a modified version of the "Dino Run" to assess its efficacy in motivating upper-limb stroke patients during repetitive training. The alteration involved changing the original horizontal movement to vertical motion, where players control a character named "Dina" to jump over obstacles representing daily activities of stroke survivors, such as eating, dressing, and bathing. The modified "Dina Run" was integrated into a comprehensive upper-limb rehabilitation program for 14 stroke patients over a period of six weeks. The system was evaluated through a pre- and post-test survey measuring motivation and engagement, alongside a comparison of training adherence between the modified "Dina Run" and the standard "Dino Run." Results indicated that the modified game significantly boosted motivation and engagement, with users reporting a preference for the modified version over the original. These findings suggest that adapting digital games to reflect the specific needs of target populations can effectively enhance adherence to repetitive rehabilitation exercises.

The user described contribution provides an Ambrosio-Tortorelli type variational framework modeling brittle fracture in piecewise-rigid materials. This work addresses two scenarios: the finite strain setting for general smooth solids and the finite strain setting restricted to linearly elastic piecewise-rigid materials.

We examine the potential for direct detection of gauge vector leptoquarks at a 100 TeV proton-proton collider, utilizing the non-universal lepton flavour anomalies observed in $B$-meson decays. Our findings indicate that these third-generation gauge vector leptoquarks, which address lepton-flavour non-universality through $SU(2)_L$ doublets, possess masses in the multi-TeV range. Consequently, they exhibit detectable signatures at future 100 Tepp colliders through dilepton final states, with sensitivities contingent upon the specific lepton-flavour non-universal anomaly considered.

Radiation exposure from positron emission tomography (PET) imaging poses potential risks to vulnerable groups, such as pregnant women and children, and can lead to unnecessary financial costs. Although the radiopharmaceuticals used in PET emit positrons that annihilate to produce gamma rays, the radiation dose is actually determined by the accompanying non-positron decay modes of the radionuclides. This study introduces a novel method to identify such modes by analyzing the energy spectra of positron annihilation radiation. The proposed approach employs a convolutional neural network (CNN) trained on simulated data generated by GEANT4 to detect non-positron decay signatures within the annihilation spectra. The model's performance was further validated using experimental data from positron emitters like $^{18}$F, $^{68}$Ga, and $^{82}$Rb. Results indicate that the CNN can accurately recognize non-positron decay modes with a 100% success rate for $^{68}$Ga and $^{82}$Rb, while achieving 99.9% accuracy for $^{18}$F.

Personalization technologies are increasingly prevalent, yet they raise significant concerns about data gathering and its subsequent use. To investigate these issues, we conducted a survey of 1,000 participants who have experience with personalized services. The survey results reveal that users are worried about data collection, how that data is utilized, and the potential for privacy breaches. Furthermore, the findings indicate that respondents are particularly concerned regarding the sharing of their information with third parties and the use of data for purposes beyond the original intent. Finally, the study highlights a need to refine future survey methodologies used to assess attitudes toward data collection and personalization.

Centering Theory (Grosz et al., 1995) serves as a framework for analyzing discourse coherence by identifying the entities about which participants talk and the topics they address. This study introduces a new method for automatically segmenting Chinese news articles into coherent units based on Centering Theory. We propose a novel, simplified algorithm that functions as an adaptation of the original Chinese version (Zhang, 2001), which was developed to address discourse segmentation in Chinese. Our approach incorporates discourse markers and the grammatical roles of nouns to enhance the original algorithm's performance. Experiments conducted on a corpus of Sina news reports demonstrate that our proposed method outperforms Zhang's (2001) approach in terms of F1 score.

We introduce the concept of an upward planar drawing for directed acyclic graphs (DAGs), defined as a planar embedding where every directed edge ascends from source to sink. Although DAGs are ubiquitous in computer science, the specific notion of "upward planarity" has received limited attention in the literature. We establish that such a drawing exists if and only if the DAG is a subgraph of some planar DAG. Furthermore, we present an $O(nm)$ algorithm to determine whether a DAG admits an upward planar representation, utilizing a technique that embeds the graph within a specific type of orthogonal structure known as a "staircase." This structure consists of a sequence of orthogonal staircases, each formed by a chain of monotonic stair segments.

The proliferation of configurable modern systems necessitates automated configuration mechanisms to enhance development cycle agility. This study introduces a novel approach to the automatic configuration of such systems by integrating a genetic algorithm with a dependency graph. This dependency graph is derived from the system's meta-model, which is typically established during the initial design phase. To validate the method, we applied it to the configuration of a Java-based Enterprise System (ESE) model. Empirical results demonstrate that this approach successfully identifies superior configurations compared to a random baseline, thereby confirming its efficacy.

We investigate operator growth within quantum systems possessing Lie symmetry, specifically those where Heisenberg-time evolution maintains symmetry. By projecting operators onto irreducible components of the system's symmetry group, we define symmetry-resolved operator growth. We specifically examine systems with $U(1)$ symmetry, demonstrating that the time evolution of symmetric components adheres to a predictable pattern characterized by a Poisson distribution. Furthermore, we establish a connection between this operator growth and the entanglement structure of symmetric quantum states, utilizing it to develop an effective model for symmetric operator growth in two-dimensional conformal field theories with $U(1)$ symmetry. These findings offer novel insights into the broader phenomenon of operator growth and its relation to quantum scrambling.

WiFi positioning is a prevalent indoor navigation technique that relies on WiFi fingerprinting, a method utilizing received signal strength indicator (RSSI) values from nearby access points. This approach typically involves two stages: an offline phase where fingerprints are gathered and an online phase where actual positioning occurs. However, the effectiveness of this process is heavily dependent on the offline phase, which is often labor-intensive and costly. Furthermore, the number of accessible access points fluctuates significantly, causing traditional methods to struggle with maintaining accuracy. To address these challenges, this study introduces a novel online positioning algorithm based on a dynamic fingerprint map. This method updates fingerprints in real-time by continuously monitoring RSSI data from surrounding access points. Additionally, the proposed algorithm employs a weighted fusion strategy to integrate multiple positioning results, thereby enhancing overall accuracy. Experimental validation confirms that this approach outperforms existing methods, particularly in environments characterized by unstable access point availability.

A Dyson Sphere represents a theoretical megastructure proposed by Freeman Dyson in 1960, intended to encompass a star and capture its radiative energy. This concept serves as a potential indicator of an advanced technological civilization within the Milky Way, offering a possible explanation for the "Fermi Paradox" by suggesting that such societies have remained undetected because they have harnessed their stars' power without emitting observable waste heat or light. While the original vision of a solid, rigid shell has largely been replaced by more plausible configurations of independent orbital components, the idea remains a cornerstone of astrobiology and the search for extraterrestrial intelligence.

Observational efforts to identify these structures rely heavily on detecting infrared excesses, which arise from the re-radiation of stellar heat by the megastructure's components. This study utilizes the Wide-field Infrared Survey Explorer (WISE) mission data to conduct a systematic search for signatures of Dyson Spheres within the Galactic disk. The methodology involves analyzing WISE all-sky data to isolate point-source stars exhibiting anomalous infrared emission relative to their optical brightness. By cross-referencing these candidates with existing databases, the analysis filters out known astrophysical phenomena such as planetary systems, debris disks, and active stellar processes.

The results indicate that the WISE dataset contains numerous sources displaying infrared excesses consistent with the thermal signatures of megastructures. However, after rigorous cross-matching and exclusion of conventional sources, the study concludes that the majority

Networked services have become a primary revenue stream for network operators, with Service Level Agreements (SLAs) serving as the formal mechanism to define these services and their quality metrics. Consequently, the effective management of SLAs is critical for network operators to sustain revenue and ensure service reliability. This paper introduces a novel resource allocation framework designed to maximize revenue from SLAs in a networked services environment. The proposed approach addresses the challenge of allocating resources to services experiencing SLA violations by employing a novel, adaptive algorithm. This algorithm utilizes a non-parametric approach to model the relationship between allocated resources and service performance, enabling the system to dynamically adjust allocations based on observed performance outcomes.

Beam breakup instability represents a significant challenge in designing high-gradient, high-field particle accelerators, ultimately capping maximum beam currents. This study introduces a novel method for analyzing beam breakup in the European X-ray Free-Electron Laser (EuXFEL) by calculating the transverse wakefield within a single cavity and subsequently determining the full wakefield through the entire structure. Our approach explicitly accounts for wakefield dispersion and incorporates the effects of beam loading. We demonstrate that this technique yields results aligning closely with those from traditional full-scale simulations.

Next-generation neutrino oscillation experiments increasingly rely on three-dimensional projection scintillator trackers, which consist of vertically stacked scintillator layers and readout strips. This paper introduces a novel method for determining the neutral current single-pion background in the Short Baseline Near Detector of the Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment (DUNE). Our approach utilizes a Monte Carlo simulation of the detector to train a convolutional neural network (CNN) to classify events by type—distinguishing between single pion, multi-pion, and muon events—based on the pattern of signals across the readout strips. We find that our CNN model can identify single-pion events with 90% efficiency. Furthermore, when integrated with a likelihood analysis, this classification capability reduces the neutral current single-pion background in a single-nu electron signal region by a factor of 2.5, with only a 10% reduction in signal efficiency.

This study examines the influence of surface water on the sticking forces between chondritic grains at different temperatures. We find that water significantly enhances sticking forces, with the effect intensifying as temperature decreases. Specifically, at 300 K, the presence of a 1 nm water layer increases the sticking force by a factor of 2.5 compared to dry conditions, whereas at 100 K, the same layer increases it by a factor of 10.5. These results indicate that water promotes sticking across all temperatures, though its impact is most pronounced at lower temperatures. Consequently, the presence of surface water does not alter the critical temperature of 150 K required for sticking to occur on dry grains; rather, it lowers this threshold to 300 K for grains coated with 1 nm of water. Additionally, we determined that a 10 nm water layer increases sticking forces by an additional factor of 2.5 relative to the 1 nm layer, suggesting that sticking forces increase linearly with water layer thickness. These findings have significant implications for understanding the sticking behavior of dust grains in the interstellar medium and protoplanetary disks.

Local Fisher Discriminant Analysis (LFDA) serves as a widely adopted technique for dimensionality reduction while maintaining class separability. This study presents a robust variant of LFDA capable of handling outliers in both data points and class centers. By utilizing a Mahalanobis distance-based kernel, this new method preserves inter-class separation even after addressing these anomalies. We offer a clear, step-by-step procedure for implementation and conduct a comparative analysis showing that this approach outperforms existing robust methods. Additionally, we apply LFDA-L to a real-world dataset to demonstrate its practical advantages.

Imitation learning stands as a powerful approach for equipping robots with complex behaviors, yet it remains challenging to apply to high-dimensional systems like humanoid platforms. Recently, extended kernelized movement primitives have emerged as an effective method for learning these behaviors from demonstrations, leveraging kernel functions to implicitly map task-level goals to goal configurations. This paper introduces a novel framework that utilizes extended kernelized movement primitives to enable humanoids to acquire behaviors from demonstrations by formulating the mapping from task goals to goal configurations as a regression problem. We demonstrate the efficacy of this framework through simulations, where a humanoid learns to walk over uneven terrain from just a few demonstrations, and through physical experiments, where a real robot successfully adapts a learned walking behavior to new starting positions.

This study examines the central emission vertex (CEV) for two gluons, a critical component of the BFKL equation within the leading logarithmic approximation. The CEV is expressed as a convolution of the three-gluon vertex with the BFKL ladder, a formulation that is subsequently simplified by applying the Lipatov approximation. This reduction reveals that the one-loop CEV is proportional to the one-loop CEV for a single gluon, with the proportionality factor being the square of the imaginary part of the BFKL Pomcutru amplitude evaluated at zero transverse momentum transfer. This finding is significant because it allows the construction of a novel, exact equation of motion for the CEV for two gluons, which holds true for the complete one-loop CEV in the massless case.

We investigate the interplay between a Zeeman field and Rashba spin-orbit coupling within a superconducting system. Our findings indicate that, under specific conditions, this combination can yield a zero-energy surface state on the Fermi surface. Furthermore, by analyzing the pairing symmetry, we demonstrate that the superconductivity transitions from an s-wave state to an extended s-wave state as the Zeeman field increases. Consequently, the emergence of a surface state at zero energy is contingent upon the coexistence of a sufficiently strong Zeeman field and a strong spin-orbit interaction strength.

We present a low-temperature specific heat analysis of La$_{2-x}$Sr$_{x}$CuO$_4$ (LSCO) with $x=0.15$, utilizing data from two samples to examine the vortex lattice across varying magnetic fields and temperatures. Our findings indicate that the vortex lattice energy scale is approximately 10 meV, consistent with prior penetration depth studies. Furthermore, we observed that increasing the magnetic field at low temperatures drives a crossover from a vortex glass state to a vortex liquid state, a behavior supported by comparisons with resistivity measurements.

This study presents a self-consistent mean-field theory for polymer brushes on substrates with radial curvature, explicitly accounting for end exclusion zones. By applying the principle of free energy minimization alongside a constraint on the total number of polymers, the model derives a closed system of coupled differential equations. Solutions indicate that radial confinement effects become increasingly significant as the product of the Flory radius and the substrate radius of curvature ($R_{\text{g}}R$) decreases. Consequently, end exclusion influences the brush's equilibrium thickness, scaling laws, and the distribution of monomers and chain ends. These theoretical predictions are validated against Monte Carlo simulations, demonstrating strong agreement.

In graph theory, the metric dimension of a graph $G$, symbolized as $\text{dim}(G)$, is defined by the minimum cardinality of its resolving sets. A resolving set $W \subseteq V(G)$ ensures that every vertex in $G$ possesses a unique distance vector relative to the elements within $W$. This study introduces the concept of a $k$-dimensional generalized resolving set (or $k$-G.R.S.), where $k$ is a positive integer, defined as a subset $W \subseteq V(G)$ such that every vertex in $G$ has at most $k$ unique distance vectors formed by $W$. We demonstrate that the minimum cardinality of any $k$-G.R.S. constitutes a new graph invariant known as the $k$-dimensional generalized metric dimension, denoted $\text{gdim}_k(G)$. Furthermore, we derive specific formulas for $\text{gdim}_k(G)$ when $G$ represents a cycle, a path, or the union of $m$ disjoint cycles.

Astronomical image quality is frequently compromised by the limitations of space-based instruments, atmospheric interference, and weather conditions. This study explores the application of machine learning to enhance the quality of astronomical images. We introduce a novel deep learning framework designed to denoise and denoise cosmic images. Our approach utilizes a convolutional neural network (CNN) trained on simulated noisy images to generate enhanced outputs from noisy inputs. We evaluated our model against two existing methods on both simulated data and real-world observations from the Hubble Space Telescope. Results indicate that our method outperforms the compared approaches, demonstrating superior performance in both quantitative metrics and visual clarity.

We introduce a novel framework for analyzing sequential decision-making in combinatorial optimization. This framework models scenarios where an agent selects an action, yielding a reward and influencing the problem's state for all subsequent decisions. We evaluate the **serial dictatorship** mechanism—a sequential selection method where agents act in a fixed order—by deriving an upper bound on the expected gap between its performance and the optimal offline solution. This bound is expressed as $O(\log n)$, where $n$ represents the count of agents. We further demonstrate that this bound is tight for a broad spectrum of problem instances. Specifically, we show that serial dictatorship achieves an expected approximation ratio of $\Omega(\log n / \log \log n)$ across various settings, including combinatorial multi-armed bandits, online submodular set packing, and online vector summation.

We present the results of a survey targeting the Main Asteroid Belt, utilizing the 1.8-meter telescope at the Leoncito American Astronomical Observatory (ALMA) to search for wide-separation binary asteroids. The survey analyzed 1,000 targets with diameters exceeding 1 km, employing a 100-second exposure time and a 1-hour total integration period. Our analysis focused on 100 of the most massive asteroids, defined as those with diameters greater than 3 km. We discovered a new binary system, 1999 AN10, characterized by a primary diameter of 3.3 km, a secondary diameter of 0.3 km, and an orbital period of 1,100 days. This discovery marks the first identified binary asteroid with a wide orbit, where the Hill radius is smaller than the orbital separation. Additionally, we determined the masses for 1999 AN10, 1999 CD5, and 1999 JU4. The confirmation of 1999 AN10 as a binary system provides crucial insights into the mechanisms of binary formation and the evolution of binary systems within the belt.

This paper presents an elementary, self-contained framework for deriving the large-sample properties of estimators and test statistics commonly found in applied econometric research. It covers both parametric and semi-parametric models, including those with fixed and increasing dimensions of nuisance parameters. The approach yields consistent and asymptotically normally distributed estimators, as well as their associated test statistics. While the primary focus is on the case where the main parameter of interest is finite-dimensional, the methods are extended to address infinite-dimensional parameters, specifically addressing the challenges posed by the resulting asymptotic distributions.

This study introduces several new findings regarding left and right Riemann-Liouville fractional integral and derivative operators. Specifically, we establish new Leibniz-style product rules, including versions with a single term, double terms, and multiple terms, as well as corresponding rules for fractional differentiation. Furthermore, we derive associated sum rules, difference rules, chain rules, and Henstock-Kakada variation of constant parameters. Additionally, we define a commutator-based product rule for these operators. Finally, we develop new inequalities connected to Henstock-Kakada variation and fractional differentiation.

This study examines the application of regularized least-squares (RLS) for demodulating user data in massive multi-access MIMO systems employing spatial modulation (SM). In the context of uplink transmission, the base station utilizes RLS to recover data from all users, while each user applies a least-squares (LS) approach for demodulation. This paper investigates the asymptotic behavior of the RLS estimator as the system dimensions grow indefinitely. Specifically, it derives the limiting conditional distribution of the squared Euclidean distance between the RLS estimate and the transmitted symbol. Leveraging this limiting distribution, the study formulates the average squared error for both the RLS estimator at the base station and the LS demodulator at the user equipment. Furthermore, a tight approximation for the conditional squared error is provided. Finally, the conditional squared error is integrated to determine the average conditional squared error, which is then utilized to optimize the regularization parameter within the RLS scheme. Numerical simulations confirm the accuracy of the proposed analytical framework.

We introduce a new, open-source Python package designed to analyze spectral energy distributions (SEDs), which are fundamental to research across astronomy. Galaxy SEDs specifically serve as crucial tools for determining galaxy properties, including stellar mass, star formation history, and dust characteristics. Although numerous tools exist for visualizing SEDs, few offer robust capabilities for data analysis. This new library addresses that gap by providing features for plotting, interpolating, and deconvolving SEDs, as well as performing statistical analyses on galaxy samples. It is built upon `astropy` and `matplotlib` to ensure compatibility with current astrophysical workflows.

The opening of the South Atlantic Atlantic generated a substantial rift basin situated between South America and Africa. This study presents a new, high-resolution, and complete 3D seismic reflection dataset covering the entire South Atlantic. This dataset was used to examine the basin's internal architecture and the associated magmatism. Our findings reveal that the basin's architecture is highly intricate, characterized by a complex interplay of rifting and magmatic processes. We propose a new classification system for the basin that divides it into three distinct domains: the South American domain, the African domain, and a transitional domain located between them. This classification is based on the relative timing of magmatic intrusions versus mechanical stretching. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the complex internal structure of the basin is the primary reason for the significant discrepancies between current geological models and seismic observations.

Unlabeled pre-training has emerged as a powerful strategy for enhancing deep learning models, particularly when labeled data is scarce. In this work, we introduce a novel unsupervised pre-training approach for Point Cloud Deep Learning (PCDL) that leverages the geometric properties of point clouds. Our method employs a self-supervised learning framework utilizing a contrastive learning objective to train point cloud representations. Specifically, we define a novel geometric contrast between points and clusters by comparing the similarity of individual points against that of clusters. This similarity is evaluated using a newly introduced metric called Geometric Contrast Entropy (GCE). To implement this, we propose two self-supervised tasks: Geometric Contrast Entropy Minimization (GCE-Min) and Geometric Contrast Entropy Maximization (GCE-Max). GCE-Min operates at the point level, whereas GCE-Max functions at the cluster level. These tasks are designed to be complementary, jointly optimizing both intra-cluster compactness and inter-cluster separation. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method yields state-of-the-art performance across various point cloud recognition and segmentation benchmarks.

We introduce a formal model for role-playing games such as Dungeons and Dragons, treating them as cooperative endeavors led by a Dungeon Master who sets objectives and designs challenges for players to overcome. We formalize these in-game activities using temporal logic and introduce a new tool, PlanDnD, which utilizes automated reasoning to support both players and Dungeon Masters. This system achieves two main goals: it assists players in discovering winning strategies to achieve their aims, and it enables Dungeon Masters to verify whether specific storylines or events are reachable within the game context.

Although the terms "change detection" and "change discovery" are often used interchangeably in lexical semantics research, this paper distinguishes them. It defines **change detection** as identifying instances of semantic change within a corpus, and **change discovery** as documenting these instances in a reference resource, such as a dictionary. This paper introduces a new dataset comprising 1,000 English semantic changes and proposes a new evaluation metric for evaluating detectors of semantic change.

We introduce new $k_\perp$-dependent functions associated with the correlation of two quark spin vectors, extending the established framework of parton distribution and fragmentation functions to include additional spin degrees of freedom. Specifically, we demonstrate that the spin-1/2 nucleon can be described by these objects as a superposition of spin configurations relative to a second quark's transverse spin. This extension applies universally to both mesons and baryons, with specific spin choices for constituent quarks within a spin-1/2 nucleon yielding twelve distinct functions, while those for spin-1/2 quarks and an anti-quark in a spin-1/2 meson result in four functions.

This study examines the statistical properties of knotoids, which are open-ended generalizations of knots, extracted from the three-dimensional structures of proteins. By utilizing the PDB database, we identified knotoid instances within proteins by mapping their backbones onto 3D space. To analyze these findings, we employed various knotoid invariants, including the minimal crossing number, the self-linking number, and the minimal push number. Our results indicate that the distribution of these properties adheres to specific statistical patterns, suggesting that knotoid characteristics serve as valuable descriptors for characterizing protein topology and geometry.

Early Dark Energy (EDE) proposes a new dark energy component that becomes significant shortly after inflation, offering a potential solution to the Hubble Tension. This study examines the cosmological evolution of EDE within the context of a scalar field coupled to dark matter via a quintessence-like mechanism. We analyze the implications of this coupling on the cosmic microwave background (CMB) and large-scale structure (LSS) by investigating the dynamics of the dark sector. Our findings indicate that the model can alleviate Hubble Tension by introducing a temporary spike in the dark energy fraction relative to radiation in the early universe. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the model remains consistent with current CMB and LSS observations.

This note demonstrates that the group of symplectic mapping classes for the one-point symplectic blowup of a manifold, where the form on S4 serves as the exception divisor, is generated by Dehn twists. This result follows from the fact that the natural Lefschetz fibration of the blowup induces a Dehn twist along a Lefschetz fiber, and the rational blowdown process allows us to track these Dehn twists under the corresponding surgery operation.

We propose a general framework for analyzing anomaly-induced modifications to the Nambu-Goldstone (NG) effective action, applicable to systems with global symmetries. This approach relies on the decomposition of the full effective action into two components: the standard part, which is determined by the global symmetry's structure constants, and an anomalous part, which is fixed by the anomaly-induced $\theta$-term. We demonstrate that this methodology is particularly effective for analyzing the interplay between global symmetries and gauge symmetries, specifically addressing the impact of gauging an anomaly-carrying symmetry on NG modes. Our findings indicate that the anomalous action modifies the standard NG matrix, resulting in a violation of the conventional Nambu-Goldstone mode counting rule. Furthermore, we show that this alteration leads to an anomalous Nambu-Goldstone theorem, which in turn modifies the Heisenberg uncertainty relation regarding the NG matrix elements. This revised uncertainty principle implies that the lower bounds on the commutator of two operators are not solely determined by the NG matrix but also by the topological term.

We introduce DISCO, a framework designed to automatically produce diverse and high-quality counterfactual samples for machine learning models. Leveraging a contrastive reinforcement learning strategy, DISCO generates data that are both effective in creating counterfactuals and diverse in their characteristics. We demonstrate through multiple experiments that DISCO significantly outperforms existing methods in generating counterfactual data, thereby enhancing model robustness against adversarial attacks and improving resilience to distributional shifts.
This paper determines the exact total chromatic number for a broad class of circulant graphs, denoted as $CI(n, \{2, d\})$, where $d$ is an odd integer greater than one.

Remote epitaxy, where a substrate's crystalline influence extends through an intervening layer to guide the growth of a third material, is a phenomenon typically limited to a few atomic distances. In this study, we demonstrate remote epitaxy across a Heusler compound, Co₂MnSi, across graphene for a substrate spacer thickness of 100 nm. Experimental evidence includes the presence of Raman G- and 2D-band shifts and the formation of a distinct interface between the graphene and the Co₂MnSi. Furthermore, the observed epitaxial alignment between the graphene lattice and the underlying substrate, persisting despite the 100 nm gap, confirms that the crystalline template effect extends significantly further than previously recorded.

This study examines the encoding maps associated with $\mathbb{Z}_p\mathbb{Z}_{p^2}$-linear block codes, which are defined as the injective homomorphisms from the additive group $\mathbb{Z}_p^u\mathbb{Z}_{p^2}^v$ into $\mathbb{Z}_p\mathbb{Z}_{p^2}$-additive block codes. The research investigates the ranks of these linear mappings and establishes that their ranks are either $uv$ or $uv+1$. Furthermore, it provides the explicit formulas for the sizes of the corresponding one-dimensional and two-dimensional subgroups of $\mathbb{Z}_p\mathbb{Z}_{p^2}$-additive block codes.

This study examines graded banks of viscosity during polymer flooding within a two-dimensional model featuring an irregular geometry and varying permeability. The objective is to evaluate the effectiveness of graded banks relative to uniform slug injection. Conditional Generative Adversarial Networks (cGANs) have become a leading approach for class-conditional generation, enabling the creation of diverse and high-quality samples across various domains. However, the effectiveness of these models relies heavily on the quality of the embedding space used to encode input conditions. This study introduces a novel architecture designed to learn continuous, semantically meaningful condition representations specifically for generative tasks. We demonstrate the utility of this method through extensive experiments on three distinct generation tasks: molecule generation, image super-resolution, and character texturing.

This paper introduces a novel, structure-preserving numerical framework for time-fractional phase-field models that incorporate energy dissipation. The approach discretizes the gradient flow equation by separating variables into a fractional time derivative within a potential well and an integer derivative on a dissipation-driven force. The coupling between these components is established via an implicit scheme for the fractional derivative, while the remaining dissipation-driven force is handled explicitly. The proposed method is validated by a rigorous proof demonstrating that the numerical scheme conserves a modified energy with corresponding modified energy dissipation inequality. Furthermore, the framework is extended to accommodate non-singular kernel functions, and numerical experiments are conducted to verify the observed energy dissipation behavior.

We begin by defining the concept of a quasi*-semi-group and demonstrating that the Gelfand-Naimark-Segal (GNS) construction can be applied to such structures using only algebraic methods. Next, we examine the set of all quasi*-representations within the framework of Gelfand-Pontryagin theory applied to the group of isometries associated with a specific class of Gelfand-Pontryagin semi-groups. Finally, we establish an algebraic version of the Gelfand-Pontryagin theorem for Gelfand-Pontryagin H*-groups.
